The Stagwell Group has made a $100m strategic equity investment into marketing and communications network MDC Partners.
The agreement comes after MDC launched a strategic review process and CEO search in September 2018.
Stagwell has purchased $50m in common shares and $50m in non-voting convertible preference shares as part of the agreement.
It will also one-time Microsoft executive Mark Penn join as chief executive of network, filling the spot of Scott Kauffman who left last year after warning about the group's profits.
The group counts 72andSunny, Anomaly, Crispin Porter Bogusky and also Forsman & Bodenfors among its stable agencies.
Presiding director of the MDC Partners' board, Irwin Simon, said: "The financial flexibility and resources provided by this investment will allow for a strengthened capital structure as well as the liquidity to selectively invest behind our world-class talent while focusing on high-priority growth areas.
"We are thrilled that this investment and Mark’s leadership will help MDC Partners reinforce its position as inspiring change-agent in our industry and home to extraordinary talent.”
On joining the company, Penn said: “I have admired MDC for a long time and believe wholeheartedly in its mission. It is home to some of the world’s best creative and strategic talent; strategists with a deep understanding of the way technology and media solutions address the needs of today’s modern marketer."
title: Stagwell Group invests $100m into MDC Partners as Mark Penn takes CEO role

Wrench Group Announces the Promotion of Dennis Laliberte to Chief Operating Officer
May 19, 2025
ATLANTA, Ga. — Wrench Group, a national leader in home services, announced the promotion of Dennis Laliberte to Chief Operating Officer, succeeding Paul Smith.
"We're excited to see Dennis step into this new role at Wrench Group," said Ken Haines, CEO of Wrench Group. "His leadership, operational expertise, and dedication to building high-performing teams have been key drivers of our success. Dennis has consistently elevated our service across markets, and we're confident he'll continue to lead our growth as we reach new milestones."
With more than 30 years of industry experience, Laliberte joined Wrench Group in 2022 as a Regional Vice President of Operations. Previously, he served as President of All About Family Home Services, parent company of Collins Comfort Masters and All About Water in the HVAC, plumbing and water filtration services and Vice President at Parker and Sons, both in the Phoenix area. Prior to those roles, he spent nearly 18 years in various leadership roles at ARS.
"I am honored to step into the role of Chief Operating Officer at Wrench Group and excited to build on the Company's incredible momentum," said Laliberte. "I want to thank Ken and the leadership team for their trust, and I want to recognize Paul for his exceptional leadership and the strong foundation he's established. I look forward to helping Wrench Group into its next phase of growth."
A home services industry veteran with almost 35 years of experience, Smith joined Wrench Group as Chief Operating Officer in 2019. Under his leadership, Wrench Group has led the industry in organic growth and launched a renowned training program that focuses on training technicians, electricians, plumbers and call center teams to better serve over 2.5 million customers a year. Smith will remain on the Executive Leadership team focused on improving critical business functions.
"We're grateful for Paul and his outstanding leadership and commitment over the past several years at Wrench Group," said Haines. "Paul has been instrumental in driving our growth to become one of the nation's top home services companies. His contributions have left a lasting mark on both our businesses and culture, and we are excited for his contributions in his new role."
About Wrench Group
Wrench Group, LLC is a national leader operating in 27 markets across 14 states. The locations provide home repair, replacement and maintenance services specializing in heating, ventilation and air conditioning, plumbing, water, electrical and related services. The company collectively serves more than 2.5 million customers annually with more than 7,400 team members.

publisher: Heat waves bump HVAC revenue by 55%, data shows, so be ready to capitalize
text:
Over the past three years, summer heat waves increased average daily revenues for HVAC businesses run on ServiceTitan by an eye-opening 55%.
That’s the takeaway from a ServiceTitan analysis that looked at how the summer heat affected companies nationwide.
» Want to grow your HVAC business? Click here for a demo
Weather events increased daily calls by 20%, jobs by 25% and revenue by 55%. In real numbers, this means that an HVAC company that averages $16,000 in revenue per day would see an additional $9,000 during the heat wave (using rounded figures).
“Fifty-five percent really grabs me,” said Chris Hunter, ServiceTitan’s Director of Customer Relations. “This means be ready for replacement opportunities and prioritize calls during the first heat wave. Most of these systems haven’t really been needed or stressed until that point, and this is where you find the systems with leaks and weak compressors.”
To grasp how much the trades are in demand when weather extremes hit, recall the 105-degree temperatures in the Northwest last summer and the freeze in Texas last February. Relief to customers leads to revenues for companies.
“Have a plan when you see the forecast, and make sure your team is ready for all hands on deck,” Hunter said. “And get your pricing correct because, with the wave of calls, this is not the time to be off on your margins.“
Record-breaking summer
ServiceTitan’s analysis looked at temperatures and KPIs from the last three years, which included one of the hottest summers on record. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration numbers showed that 2021 matched the Dust Bowl summer of 1936. From June’s record-breaking heat in the southern and western states to the mid-August dual heat waves that affected both the western and the eastern parts of the country, the weather was relentless.
The #1 newsletter for the trades.
When gathering data, ServiceTitan defined a heat wave as two or more days when the temperature was unusually hot for an area, and the heat did not relent at night. Last year, some ZIP codes in San Antonio saw the first heat wave on June 7 and 8, when night temperatures remained above 78 degrees for two days in a row. In California, Canoga Park saw its first heat wave on July 19-22, when night temperatures did not cool below 70.
ServiceTitan analyzed proprietary data on approximately 800 HVAC shops along with detailed records from weather stations to determine the increase in calls, jobs, and revenue from the heat waves. A deeper dive analyzed the timing of the heat waves within the season and the geographical differences between regions.
First heat wave vs. fifth? Big difference
The impact on daily revenue was clear with the 55% increase.
What was just as clear was the first heat wave of the season has a much larger impact on revenue than subsequent weather events.
Figure 1. Average Impact of Heat Waves on Daily Revenue, by Order Within a Season
Compared to a baseline of a summer day without a heat wave, the first temperature event increases daily revenue by about 90%, which is about two-thirds more than the second and more than double the third. By the time the fifth heat wave of the season arrives, daily revenue increases by only 20%, on average. The impact after the fifth is often at or near zero in many regions.
That company with $16,000 per day in revenue? The increase from the first heat wave would be $14,000. The second would be $8,500, the fifth $3,000.
“This means just because the cash is rolling in after the first heat wave doesn’t mean anyone should make frivolous spending decisions,” Hunter said. “Communicate this trend to the team so they don’t get so overwhelmed and burnt out after the first couple of heat waves. Schedule vacations or R&R later in the season if possible.”
Location, location, location
Where the heat wave hits also matters. Temperature domes in the Northwest, Upper Rockies and far West tend to have a far greater impact on revenue than similar weather events in the South or Midwest.
HVAC shops in the West and Northwest see much bigger impacts on their KPIs than the shops in the South and Southeast. Weather, HVAC systems and housing types vary substantially across regions, which means the magnitude of the impacts vary as well. Think about Portland and Seattle, and all the stories last year about how the 100-degree temperatures were hitting areas that did not typically have air conditioning.
Over the past three years, the Northwest experienced a 120% increase in daily revenue for work booked during heat waves. The Northern Rockies and Plains (Nebraska, Montana) and West (California, Nevada) saw increases of 100%.
By contrast, shops in the South and Southeast increased daily revenue by 40% and 30%. There, homes already have HVAC units installed.
“I would really pick up the branding before the heat wave hits,” Hunter said. “Some contractors wait until they get busy to market, and by then they could be just wasting dollars.
“I want to be top of mind with my customers, so that way at the first sign of discomfort, it’s a no-brainer who to call for fast, professional service.”
Charge based on demand?
Hunter said he thinks it wise to consider adjusting pricing based on demand.
“Airlines, Uber and hotels have dynamic pricing due to demand,” he said. “A contractor could consider this as well. A slight price increase in the busiest season will produce more profit. Also some contractors may charge a premium for front-of-the-line service and homeowners are willing to pay this.
“We only have so many jobs, might as well make those jobs the most profitable ones.
“Finally, the busy season is a great time to lock in new memberships. Especially if your membership plan provides priority service and you can make them a member and give that benefit right away.”
[Methods: ServiceTitan followed Environmental Protection Agency standards in defining a heat wave. The summer season is defined as May through August. Weather data comes from the Global Surface Summary of the Day (GSOD) dataset. Final numbers were from a three-year average from 2019-2021 and rounded to the nearest 5%.]
ServiceTitan Software
ServiceTitan is a comprehensive software solution built specifically to help service companies streamline their operations, boost revenue, and substantially elevate the trajectory of their business. Our comprehensive, cloud-based platform is used by thousands of electrical, HVAC, plumbing, garage door, and chimney sweep shops across the country—and has increased their revenue by an average of 25% in just their first year with us.

Industry: Transportation and Logistics, ERP: Microsoft Great Plains, Products in use: Invoice Processing, Bill of Lading (BOL) Matching, Approvals, Payments, Advanced Analytics
AP cost and time savings driven by:
- 99% accuracy in invoice coding and classification
- Achieving a no-touch invoice processing rate of 84%
- Shortening the AP financial close process from 4 to 3 days
- Reassigning 3 FTEs to focus on higher-value departmental activities
Download the Diesel Direct case study
Diesel Direct, a leading fuel delivery and transportation company headquartered in Massachusetts with customers in all 50 states, has transformed its financial operations and realized a significant ROI by adopting Vic.ai for autonomous invoice processing and bill pay. With multiple operating brands and a complex network of fuel deliveries, Diesel Direct faced significant challenges in scaling and managing its accounts payable (AP) processes without adding headcount. The company also struggled to accurately present AP on its balance sheet on a timely basis, requiring time-consuming manual accruals by its accounting department. This case study examines how the company overcame these obstacles, realized near-immediate ROI, and achieved remarkable improvements in its financial operations through advanced AI.
Prior state and business challenges
Before adopting Vic.ai, Diesel Direct's AP department struggled to keep up with recording the volume of invoices and payments. Andrew Turkish, VP and Corporate Controller at Diesel Direct, describes the situation: "Our AP state of affairs was, to be quite honest, always a fire drill. We probably had 100 or more unread emails in our inbox at any given time. So we were constantly in a backlog position."
The company used a template-based document management and workflow software, which proved inflexible and prone to errors. Turkish explains, "Every time a vendor tweaked their invoice, the template broke. And we had to spend time redeveloping that template to get efficiency from it."
The situation was particularly problematic when dealing with fuel suppliers who would auto-draft payments upon the due date. Turkish elaborates, "If we were behind on processing their invoices being emailed to us, slowly but surely, we're going to get into a debit balance because they're going to debit the vendor weekly for the payments. And we're not processing the credits timely (for the invoices) to zero out."
Process inefficiencies drained money
In addition to the manual effort to maintain an accurate balance sheet, Diesel Direct faced multiple automation challenges for managing incoming invoices and processing payments, which caused delays and unnecessary costs:
1. Constant invoice backlog: The AP mailbox regularly had over 100 unread emails containing invoices, leading to debit balances in our AP subledger and a significant challenge in managing DPO and related analytics. This backlog created a snowball effect, as the AP team struggled to catch up while new invoices continued to arrive daily.
2. Manual and time-consuming invoice processing: Their template-based software was inflexible and prone to errors. Even minor changes in vendor invoices would break the template, requiring time-consuming manual intervention and template redevelopment. This inefficiency significantly slowed down the entire AP process and caused frustration for the AP staff.
3. Inefficient payment systems: The company's check payment process was particularly cumbersome. AP analysts spent four to six hours printing checks, obtaining signatures, and stuffing envelopes every Friday. This manual process not only consumed valuable time but also increased the risk of manual errors, risking a delay for vendor payments.
4. Difficulty presenting accurate financial positions: Due to the invoice backlog and inefficient processes, Diesel Direct's AP balance often appeared in a debit position on the balance sheet. While mitigated via accruals, this complicated interactions with auditors and financial institutions.
5. Challenges in scaling AP operations: As Diesel Direct grew, they faced difficulties in integrating and centralizing AP operations. Any acquisition or significant growth required additional AP support, as the Diesel Direct AP team could not absorb the additional workload. This approach hindered standardization efforts and increased operational costs.
To reduce invoice processing errors, improve balance sheet accuracy for real-time forecasting, and implement true automation without human intervention, Turkish knew Diesel Direct needed to rethink its operational AP approach and reevaluate the technology in use.
Evolving to an AI-first solution
Recognizing the need for a more robust solution, Turkish sought assistance from a trusted partner with experience in software sourcing. After a thorough evaluation of various software options. "They came back with raving reviews about Vic.ai," Turkish recalls. This recommendation prompted Turkish to reach out directly to Vic.ai for a demonstration.
During the vendor selection process, Turkish was particularly impressed by the comprehensive nature of Vic.ai's offering. Unlike other point solutions focused solely on invoice processing, Vic.ai presented a holistic approach to financial operations.
"It wasn't just an invoice ingestion AP software," Turkish explains. "Vic.ai to me was not just about what they offered at the time but also where they were going. You have all these different modules that can take me from start to finish and more."
This end-to-end solution capability, combined with the projected headcount efficiencies, set Vic.ai apart from other vendors and aligns well with Diesel Direct's goals for financial transformation.
The Vic.ai platform
Diesel Direct implemented several key components of the Vic.ai platform: Invoice Processing, Bill of Lading (BOL) matching, Approval Flows, Payments, Advanced Analytics.
The Vic.ai platform integrates directly with Diesel Direct's ERP system, Microsoft Great Plains, enabling a seamless flow of financial data across the organization. The integration allows for real-time synchronization of invoice data, payment information, and financial records between Vic.ai and Great Plains. This interconnectivity eliminated the need for manual data entry, reduced errors, and provided a single source of truth for financial reporting and analysis.
The implementation of Vic.ai has had a significant impact on AP processes for Diesel Direct, all of which contribute tangible savings and measurable improvements:
1. Invoice Ingestion: All invoices now go through Vic.ai, posting and integrating directly into Great Plains.
2. Bill of Lading (BOL) matching: BOL documents are automatically matched at 99 percent accuracy rates using Vic.ai’s PO matching functionality.
3. Workflow standardization: Approvals for general invoices have been standardized across the organization.
4. Payments execution: Payments are now being executed through Vic.ai and integrated directly into the ERP system.
5. Analytics and reporting: The platform provides real-time analytics on invoice processing data, team performance, and business trends.
The tangible ROI of an AI-driven approach
Meeting the goals they had set for improving efficiency and scalability, Diesel Direct also realized efficiencies of three FTEs.
Headcount efficiency gains have been realized, leading Turkish to extend the Vic.ai contract: Turkish reports, "Our initial business case said we would achieve three FTE efficiencies from going live with this. I'm happy to say that we're somewhere around two and a half today, and I'm expecting we'll hit our three FTE efficiencies once the rest of our entities get on the payments module."
These efficiency gains and annual savings were afforded by the tangible benefits of implementing Vic.ai, including:
Faster invoice processing: The Diesel Direct team has seen a 65% reduction in invoice processing time. By month six, they had also achieved a 99% accuracy rate in all relevant invoice information, including vendor, dates, GL coding, BOL, and dimensions, further supporting a more efficient and reliable process. This saved the team both time and money previously locked up in manual work.
Payment processing automation: Leveraging Vic.ai Payments has transformed their manual process. The AP team spent hours printing, signing, and mailing checks each week, draining the equivalent of 0.5 FTEs per month. Turkish has already seen significant time savings across the entities using payments today and anticipates further efficiencies once the remaining entities are live. “Vic.ai eliminated all the manual components of our payments process, providing each AP analyst with an additional 3 to 6 hours of capacity each week,” Turkish says.
Improved financial clarity: The accurate processing of invoices has stopped the snowball effect of the previous issue regarding the AP balance appearing in a debit position. This has significantly improved Diesel Direct's efficiency in presenting its financial position to auditors, rating agencies, and banks, saving hours of time each month recording manual accruals.
Time savings: "One of the things this did was shorten our AP close process by a day. Our AP team was closing on workday four. They now close on workday three without the need to make significant accruals," Turkish explains.
Scalability: The Vic.ai platform has allowed Diesel Direct to centralize its AP operations across multiple entities. Turkish highlights, "It is now much easier to scale for growth and set up new entities and brands in Vic.ai through our established process." This means Diesel Direct can continue to grow more efficiently and add much less headcount against AP workflows, while maintaining the speed and accuracy of their new efficiency benchmarks with Vic.ai.
Improved employee satisfaction: The AP team has embraced the Vic.ai platform. Turkish shares, "I was pleasantly surprised and they all fully love the usability and the friendliness of the software."
Future platform expansion and automation goals
Looking ahead, Diesel Direct plans to fully implement the payments module across all entities, which will bring additional time savings. Turkish anticipates, "Every Friday is check day, taking each AP analyst four to six hours to print checks, get them signed, and stuff envelopes. Payments will drive significant time savings."
The company also sees potential for further leveraging Vic.ai's capabilities for treasury functions and cash flow forecasting.
As Diesel Direct continues to grow, the scalability offered by Vic.ai will play a crucial role in maintaining efficient financial operations across the expanding organization, while maintaining a lean AP team.
The implementation of Vic.ai has not only solved Diesel Direct's immediate AP challenges but has also positioned the company for future growth and financial stability. By leveraging AI-powered accounting solutions, Diesel Direct has transformed its financial operations, improving efficiency, accuracy, and strategic decision-making capabilities.

Chad Simpson, Founder, Simpson Heating & Air

Metric of the Month:
First Level Resolution Rate
By Jeff Rumburg
Every month, in the Industry Insider, I highlight one key performance indicator (KPI) for the
service desk or desktop support. I define the KPI, provide recent benchmarking data for the
metric, and discuss key correlations and cause/effect relationships for the metric. The purpose
of the column is to familiarize you with the KPIs that really matter to your support organization,
and to provide actionable insight on how to leverage these KPIs to improve your performance.
First Level Resolution Rate
First level resolution (FLR) is a measure of a service desk’s ability to resolve tickets at level 1,
without having to escalate the ticket to level 2 (desktop support), level 3 (internal IT professionals
in applications, networking, the data center, or elsewhere), field support, or vendor support. But
first level resolution is not to be confused with its close cousin, first contact resolution. Let me
provide an example to illustrate the difference.
Take the situation where a level 1 agent accepts a call and logs a ticket, but fails to provide a
solution to the caller on the initial contact. Rather than escalate the ticket, the level 1 agent
researches the user’s issue, identifies an appropriate solution, calls the user back, delivers the
solution, and closes out the ticket. Although the ticket was not resolved on the first contact, it
was resolved at level 1. Now, let’s take the situation where the level 1 agent accepts a call, logs a
ticket, and warm transfers the caller to a level 3 IT professional who works in the NOC. The level
3 professional takes over the call and provides a solution for the ticket before the user hangs up.
This ticket was resolved on first contact, but was not resolved at the first level.
It is also helpful to note that first contact resolution is a quality metric that strongly affects
customer satisfaction, while first level resolution is a cost metric that strongly influences total cost
of ownership for end-user support.
Net vs. Gross FLR
To have a meaningful discussion of FLR, we have to make a further distinction between gross first
level resolution and net first level resolution. Gross FLR is the ratio of all tickets resolved at level 1
to all tickets logged at level 1. Net FLR, by contrast, is the ratio of all tickets resolved at level 1 to
all tickets that can potentially be resolved at level 1.

2© 2011 MetricNet, LLC and United Business Media LLC. All rights reserved.
Gross FLR is self-explanatory . It is a simple ratio that, for most people, is very intuitive. However,
to fully appreciate net FLR, we must define the term carve-out. A carve-out is a ticket type that
for one reason or another cannot be resolved at level 1. A carve-out can be the result of a physical
limitation (e.g., it is physically impossible to replace a hardware component remotely at level 1),
or it might be the result of policy or security restrictions placed on level 1 support, such as when
level 1 is denied access rights to certain systems. The denominator of the net FLR ratio is equal to
the number of tickets logged at level 1 minus the number of carve-outs.
Net FLR is by far the more important of the two metrics, for it measures the true effectiveness of
the level 1 service desk to resolve tickets within their purview of defined responsibility .
First Level Resolution and Total Cost of Ownership
Figure 1 illustrates the cost per ticket for resolution at different support levels. This data represents
North American averages and is a fully-burdened cost, including agent salaries and benefits, salaries
and benefits for indirect personnel (e.g., trainers, workforce schedulers, etc.), facilities expenses
(i.e., rent, lease, or depreciation for the occupied facilities), insurance, telecommunications,
desktop technology (e.g., licensing fees, desktop/laptop computers, etc.), travel, training, and
office supplies. Clearly , as a ticket is escalated, and resolution moves further away from the level 1
service desk, the cost of resolution increases. Furthermore, these costs are cumulative. If a ticket
is logged at level 1 and then escalated to level 2 (desktop support) for resolution, the average cost
of resolution is not just $62, but $62 plus $22, for a total of $84.
The cost of resolution increases at each successive level for a number of reasons, including longer
handle times and higher salaries at support levels above the service desk. So, for example, a
ticket that might be resolved in ten minutes at level 1 could take thirty minutes or more at level 2
because it requires a visit to the user’s location. The same ticket, when resolved at level 3, involves
personnel that are more highly paid than level 1 agents, and who are (frankly) slower to resolve
tickets because they are not full-time support professionals. The clear implication is that any
ticket that can be resolved at level 1 should be resolved at level 1, and that maximizing FLR is the
equivalent of minimizing TCO!

3© 2011 MetricNet, LLC and United Business Media LLC. All rights reserved.

Benchmark Ranges for Net FLR
MetricNet’s benchmarking database shows that the average net FLR for service desks worldwide
is about 74 percent. This number varies widely , however, from a low of about 38 percent to a
high of 98 percent. Those at the low end of this range are predominantly log-and-dispatch service
desks that resolve simple issues, such as password resets, but dispatch anything more complex to
a higher level of support. Those performing at the upper end of this range generally have highly
trained agents that are equipped with tools that enable them to resolve more than 90 percent of
eligible contacts at level 1 (e.g., knowledge management systems, remote diagnostic capabilities,
etc.).
Figure 2 shows the distribution of FLR statistics for a representative cross-section of service desks
worldwide.

Complete Legal’s Acquisition of Frontline Managed Service’s eDiscovery Unit: Setting a Client-Centric Standard in Legal Tech
ComplexDiscovery Staff
In a strategic move that reinforces its position in the legal technology sector, Complete Legal, a prominent independent litigation support firm, has announced the acquisition of Frontline Managed Service’s eDiscovery unit. This acquisition follows Complete Legal’s recent merger with L2 Services and Precise Legal, reflecting a concerted effort to expand its expertise in eDiscovery, information governance, and data management.
Frontline Managed Service’s eDiscovery unit, known for its proficiency in delivering comprehensive eDiscovery services under long-term contracts, represents a significant addition to Complete Legal’s talent pool. This integration is a response to the increased demand for specialized skills following Complete Legal’s expansion through mergers.
In an announcement of the acquisition, Eric Singer, CEO of Complete Legal, emphasized the strategic importance of this acquisition in scaling the company’s services to meet the needs of a growing client base. The move is seen as a key element in enhancing the firm’s operational capacity and service delivery in the eDiscovery domain.
Additionally, Chief Operating Officer Eric Kelting acknowledged the dual benefits of the acquisition, citing not only the infusion of skilled talent but also the expansion of the firm’s client roster. This development is expected to significantly scale Complete Legal’s ability to support clients’ diverse eDiscovery, information governance, and data management requirements.
Also, Chief Strategy Officer Jeff Dreiling outlined the acquisition as a step towards realizing a broader vision of delivering top-tier discovery services to a wider client base. He highlighted the alignment in client service philosophies between Complete Legal and Frontline’s unit, noting the shared emphasis on building deep, long-term client relationships that add value.
The Nashville-based Frontline Managed Services eDiscovery unit, operating remotely with a distributed team across the United States, will continue to function from its Nashville office, with all employees retained. This decision ensures continuity and leverages the unit’s established expertise.
Complete Legal’s acquisition of Frontline Managed Service’s eDiscovery unit marks a notable development in the eDiscovery industry. It not only enhances Complete Legal’s capabilities but also showcases the firm’s commitment to meeting the evolving needs of its clients through strategic growth and talent acquisition. This move also may indicate a continued trend of consolidation in the legal technology sector, with firms increasingly seeking to broaden their service offerings and client base.

One Hour SPE in state court, bringing claims for declaratory judgment, breach of contract, conversion, and
misappropriation of trade secrets. The lawsuit arose from disputes over (1) the validity of the post -term
covenant against competition contained in the Franchise Agreement, which expired in July 2021, (2)
whether One Hour SPE failed to provide the former franchisee an agreed -upon territory in one of the
Franchise Agreements, and (3) whether One Hour SPE denied the franchisee access to a customer database.
The complaint sought a declaratory judgment that the covenant against competition was invalid and
unspecified compensatory damages. The complaint also sought punitive damages and attorneys’ fees on
the conversion and trade secrets claims and treble damages on the trade secrets claim. One Hour SPE
removed the lawsuit to federal court and, on September 14, 2021, filed a counterclaim seeking to enjoin the

Independent Fashion & Apparel Sales Representative (1099 - 15% Commission)
About Us We are a premier apparel manufacturing and wholesale group. As a factory-direct manufacturer, we control the entire supply chain from design to production. We represent a diverse and growing portfolio of established fashion brands specifically curated for the mid-to-premium contemporary market.
By eliminating all middlemen, we deliver premium-quality, on-trend fashion collections to retailers at highly competitive, manufacturer-direct wholesale prices, offering incredible value to upscale boutiques without compromising on quality or production ethics.
To accelerate our US expansion, we are seeking well-connected Independent Sales Representatives (1099) to introduce our multi-brand portfolio to contemporary boutiques and premium retail stores nationwide.
The Opportunity This is a pure commission-based (1099) contract role, perfectly suited for established multi-line sales reps who want to add a powerful, high-margin, premium apparel manufacturer to their current portfolio.
Instead of selling just one single brand, you will have access to our entire multi-brand fashion ecosystem (covering casual wear, premium denim, and more), allowing you to maximize your sales volume and easily cross-sell to your existing boutique clients.
While the industry standard commission for premium apparel is 10-12%, we offer a premier 15% commission on all wholesale orders because we believe in rewarding the top-tier talent that drives our growth.
Key Responsibilities
- Introduce and pitch our mid-to-premium apparel collections (Lilax, CBDenim, etc.) to independent contemporary boutiques, specialty stores, and premium retail buyers across the US.
- Leverage your existing retail network and book of business to secure wholesale placement.
- Present digital lookbooks, line sheets, and product catalogs to prospective buyers.
- Manage the B2B sales process from initial outreach to closing the wholesale order.
- Maintain strong, long-term relationships with retail clients to encourage consistent re-orders.
What We Are Looking For
- Established Network: You must have an active, proven book of business with independent mid-to-premium fashion boutiques, contemporary apparel retailers, or specialty stores in the US.
- Industry Experience: Minimum 2+ years of successful B2B sales experience in the contemporary fashion, premium apparel, or textile wholesale industry.
- Independent Mindset: You are a self-motivated 1099 contractor who thrives with a flexible, independent schedule (estimated 40 hours per month).
What We Offer
- 15% Commission Rate: Industry-leading, uncapped commission structure paid promptly on closed orders based on premium-market order values.
- The Manufacturer-Direct Edge: Highly competitive factory pricing on premium-quality goods, giving you a massive competitive advantage.
- Multi-Brand Catalog: High cross-selling potential with diverse contemporary brands under one manufacturing umbrella.
- Sales Support: We provide high-quality product photography, professional digital line sheets, and seamless order fulfillment from our manufacturing hubs.
If you have the connections and want to leverage a true factory-direct partnership in the US mid-to-premium market, we want to partner with you. Apply today to discuss how we can grow together!

Thaddeus Stevens College expands workforce training to North Philadelphia
Lancaster-based Thaddeus Stevens College of Technology is launching a training location with Esperanza Tec Centro Philadelphia.
It marks the newest location in the Tec Centro Workforce Network on Esperanza’s multi-service campus in Hunting Park, North Philadelphia. Thaddeus Stevens College has operated short-term training as part of its Workforce and Economic Development Center for about a decade and is expanding those trainings into a new region. Enrollment is open for upcoming information sessions.
“It has always been the mission of Thaddeus Stevens College to create access and opportunity for education,” Pedro Rivera, president of Thaddeus Stevens College of Technology, said in a statement. “Partnering with deeply embedded community organizations such as Esperanza, known for its dedication to uplifting the community in tangible ways, as well as Tec Centro, focused on training to open doors for a bright future, we couldn’t envision a better relationship to establish the College’s presence in Philadelphia.
“Together, we are excited to offer a curriculum and a chance for those looking to build a stable, meaningful career.”
The workforce training center is the seventh site in the statewide network and will provide adult basic education and no-cost career training in high-demand skilled trades for unemployed and underemployed adults. The opening of Esperanza Tec Centro Philadelphia is possible through funding received by the Tec Centro Workforce Network, a 501(c)(3) organization. The funds provided to the network support the opening of new centers, construction, outfitting, and workforce training.
According to a release, Esperanza brings nearly 20 years of workforce development experience helping Philadelphians access employment opportunities. The new site will expand access to workforce training while helping meet the demand for skilled workers in industries throughout the region.
Programs launching at Esperanza Tec Centro Philadelphia, in partnership with Thaddeus Stevens College, include Metals Fabrication and Welding Technology, Commercial-Industrial HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, and Air-Conditioning), Commercial-Industrial Plumbing, and Facility Maintenance Technology. Programs are open to adults 18 and older in the Philadelphia area seeking career opportunities, including individuals from all backgrounds and experience levels. No prior training is required. ESL and GED classes will also be available for participants seeking to strengthen foundational skills.
Construction and final preparations for Esperanza Tec Centro Philadelphia have begun, with workforce training programs expected to start after the center’s completion this summer. The first student cohorts are expected to launch at the end of this month.
Esperanza Tec Centro Philadelphia is a collaboration between Esperanza, the Tec Centro Workforce Network and the Workforce & Economic Development Center at Thaddeus Stevens College of Technology. The new center expands access to workforce education and career pathways for adults across Philadelphia while helping meet local workforce demands.
“By ensuring individuals have access to family-sustaining jobs, we continue to fulfill our vision of an opportunity community where everyone has access to economic mobility and a good quality of life,” said Rev. Danny Cortés, executive vice president and chief operating officer of Esperanza. “By addressing remaining gaps in access to training and job placement opportunities in these growing trades, this initiative will be a vital contributor to the overall health and economic vitality of Philadelphia and the region.”
The launch of Esperanza Tec Centro Philadelphia marks another milestone in the Tec Centro Workforce Network’s mission to expand community-based workforce training across Pennsylvania and connect more residents to family-sustaining careers.
“Esperanza Tec Centro Philadelphia represents exactly what the Tec Centro Workforce Network was created to accomplish, which is bringing together trusted community organizations, educational institutions, employers, and local leaders to expand opportunity where it is needed most,” said Carlos Graupera, president and CEO of the Tec Centro Workforce Network. “Every new center strengthens our statewide network while creating new pathways to family-sustaining careers for individuals and stronger workforces for the communities we serve. We are proud to welcome Esperanza as the newest partner in this growing movement,”

text:
Abstract
Cooling degree days (CDD) are widely used to estimate air-conditioning energy demand, yet they implicitly assume constant refrigeration efficiency, neglecting its dependence on temperature and humidity. We introduce an efficiency-aware cooling metric –effective cooling degree days (eCDD)– that links ambient temperature and humidity to the physical work required for cooling. Here we show that, across North America, cooling efficiency has declined by 2–4% per decade since 1971, and that regionally opposing trends in temperature and humidity cause CDD to misrepresent cooling demand. During hot extremes, efficiency losses are amplified under humid-heat but partially offset under dry-heat. Projections reveal a continent-scale shift in humidity regimes, with an eastward extension of dry heat that enhances cooling efficiency during extremes, while eCDD increases by 10–80%. These results demonstrate that temperature-based metrics alone are insufficient and efficiency-aware metrics are essential for accurately assessing cooling demand, especially considering differing electricity generation mixes.
Subject terms: Environmental impact, Atmospheric science
A metric shows air conditioners work less efficiently as temperatures rise, while humidity can worsen or offset losses. Across North America, future cooling energy demand may grow far faster than standard temperature-based estimates suggest.
Introduction
Cooling infrastructure underpins public health, economic activity, and global cold-chain logistics, and its importance is intensifying as exposure to heat and humidity increases1–3. The air-conditioning (AC) sector is now a nearly $100 billion (USD) market with about 100 million units sold each year, and household AC penetration is projected to rise from 27% to 41%, increasing residential cooling electricity demand from 1220 to 1940 terawatt-hours (TWh) year−14–6, trajectories that threaten power-system reliability and amplify household energy burdens.
Cooling degree days (CDD), defined as the cumulative temperature exceedance above a base threshold, are widely used as a proxy for cooling demand, implicitly assuming equal energy requirement per degree. The metric was originally developed as an analog to heating degree days, rather than from first-principles cooling physics7. This requires system efficiency to remain constant, even though ambient temperature and humidity jointly control the vapor-compression cycle efficiency. Recent extensions that use wet-bulb temperature, humidity, or population weighting8–10 improve how CDD is represented but still treat all degrees of exceedance as thermodynamically equivalent. By ignoring efficiency changes, CDD conflates thermal forcing with required work, introducing a state-dependent bias in energy demand estimates.
Cooling efficiency is governed by vapor-compression thermodynamics and by the partitioning of heat between sensible and latent components. Rising temperatures increase the thermodynamic lift required for heat rejection, reducing system performance, while higher humidity further degrades efficiency by diverting capacity toward latent heat removal. As a result, hot-dry conditions primarily penalize cooling through increased compressor work, whereas hot-humid conditions impose an additional loss by suppressing sensible cooling. Cooling demand metrics that ignore these efficiency variations provide an incomplete representation of cooling demand. Consistent with this framework, experiments show efficiency losses of 40–54% across operating conditions, compounding electricity use and peak load stress11–13.
Therefore, projecting cooling demand requires metrics that reflect the physical work performed by cooling systems, rather than temperature exceedance alone. Here we introduce a thermodynamically-informed reframing of cooling demand metrics that links ambient thermal conditions directly to the thermodynamic effort required for cooling. By accounting for how temperature and humidity jointly govern cooling-system efficiency, we replace the implicit constant-efficiency assumption embedded in conventional cooling degree days. This framework yields an efficiency-aware cooling demand metric – effective cooling degree days (eCDD) – that transforms cooling degree days from a purely temperature-based index into a thermodynamically meaningful measure of cooling work. Using this approach across North America, we show that conventional temperature-based metrics systematically mischaracterize cooling demand, motivating a shift from empirical degree-day proxies to physics-based cooling demand indicators.
Results
Climatic controls of cooling efficiency
Cooling efficiency is fundamentally state-dependent, rather than constant, with the Coefficient of Performance (COP, the ratio of heat removed to work input) reflecting temperature-dependent compressor performance, and the Sensible Heat Ratio (SHR) describing the partitioning between sensible temperature reduction and latent moisture removal. Both COP and SHR are strongly governed by local climate conditions (Fig. 1a, b). COP has declined by up to 4% per decade over the last five decades for the months of May to September (MJJAS), with particularly strong decreases in areas along the western flank of the Rocky Mountains. Simultaneously, SHR trends exhibit strong regional variability, with some areas (e.g., the Great Basin, Pacific and Central Southwest) showing increases of 1.5–3%, while others (e.g., U.S. Northern Plains) show decreases of 1.5–3%, with similar structure to trends in relative humidity14.
This interaction produces a “tug-of-war” between the impacts of refrigeration load on the compressor and the balance between latent and sensible heat removal, where efficiency loss from COP can be amplified or offset by decreases or increases in SHR (Fig. 1c). To capture the interaction between SHR and COP, we define an effective coefficient of performance (eCOP, COP multiplied by SHR, see Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2). eCOP has declined by approximately 1.6–2.4% per decade across much of the United States, with some regions experiencing declines of over 8% per decade (e.g., western Canada, Fig. 1d). Surprisingly, other areas, such as the Pacific Southwest, show negligible or even positive trends (though statistically insignificant) when accounting for the offsetting by SHR.
To capture the relationship of cooling energy demand with efficiency, we create the efficiency-weighted cooling degree days (eCDD), defined as CDD divided by eCOP (Fig. 2; Supplementary Fig. 2). Summertime eCDD has increased by 4–12% per decade over most of North America, with certain regions over the Rockies exceeding 20% per decade (Fig. 2a). Importantly, conventional CDD overestimates the trend in cooling demand by ~1.2–2.7% per decade, especially in parts of the Pacific Southwest (Fig. 2b), which amounts to almost a 50% overestimation over the regions’ 6–10% per decade CDD trend (Supplementary Fig. 3).
Conversely, across much of the Southeast and central United States, CDD underestimates trends by up to 3% per decade (Fig. 2b). Regions of significant over- and underestimation align with long-term trends in SHR (Fig. 1b), indicating that CDD performs poorly where SHR trends are substantial. The shortcoming of CDD is further shown near anomalous regional climate dynamics, such as with central U.S. warming hole, where daily maximum temperature have remained constant or decreased15. Here, CDD trends are weak, as temperature alone is considered, yet produces significantly different eCDD trends. Overall, these results demonstrate that conventional CDD fails to capture key regional differences in cooling demand, and that efficiency weighting is required for regions where temperature and inlet moisture stress evolve jointly.
During extreme events, defined here as days with temperature exceeding the 95th percentile, many areas southeast of the Central Plains have a lower eCDD anomaly when compared to much of Canada, U.S. Pacific Northwest, Great Basin, and Northern Rockies, which have elevated eCDD anomalies that are up to 3 standard deviations (Fig. 2c). The differences with efficiency weighting CDD (Fig. 2d) closely tracks with the response of both SHR and eCOP (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). Where extreme heat coincides with positive SHR anomalies (drier conditions), CDD tends to overestimate cooling demand, whereas in regions with accompanying negative SHR anomalies (wetter conditions) the discrepancy reverses sign. This asymmetry reflects CDD’s assumption of fixed cooling efficiency: for eCDD, reduced inlet moisture stress increases SHR and lowers the effective cooling penalty, whereas increased inlet moisture stress reduces SHR and raises it. Here, dry and humid heat extremes arise from differences in land-atmosphere coupling, with radiation-driven forcing producing dry events under soil-moisture limitation and humid events where evaporation remains active16.
The importance of distinguishing inlet moisture stress (i.e., vapor pressure) from the relative humidity in shaping the SHR anomaly is exemplified by the 1995 Chicago and 2012 Central U.S. heat waves (Supplementary Fig. 5 and 6). For both events, anomalously high saturation vapor pressure indicated a thermodynamic capacity for vapor pressure to increase, provided sufficient moisture was available in the surrounding environment. During the 1995 event, vapor pressure rose at approximately the same rate as the saturation vapor pressure, resulting in increased inlet moisture stress, while the relative humidity anomaly was essentially flat. This produced a negative SHR anomaly and anomalously high eCDD compared with CDD. Conversely, in 2012 vapor pressure was anomalously low resulting in decreased inlet moisture stress and anomalously high SHR, as well as a negative relative humidity, leading to anomalously low eCDD compared to CDD. Thus, these two cases show that relying solely on the relative humidity to understand how eCDD will evolve is insufficient and that one must consider the role of inlet moisture stress in determining SHR and, consequently, eCDD.
Projections of effective cooling demand
Model simulations show that the response of eCDD to a high emissions scenario by mid-century (2015-2050) is projected to increase 10–80% across most of the continent and particularly large increases of up to 150% in northern regions (Fig. 3a). These regions of extreme increase occur in areas where there have historically been minimal cooling degree days (Supplementary Fig. 7), consistent with past studies17,18. Furthermore, compared with CDD, eCDD is expected to increase more rapidly across essentially all of North America, including an average of 7.5–15.0% over much of the U.S., with large anomalies of over 30% in northern regions (i.e., Alaska, Yukon, British Columbia, Fig. 3b, and Supplementary Fig. 7 for full fields).
Over the Central U.S. regions, eCDD outpaces CDD less strongly than in surrounding regions, although it remains statistically significant in the multi-model analysis. This region of reduced divergence likely reflects compensating effects between SHR trends and declining compressor efficiency (COP), which occur over similar areas (Supplementary Fig. 7c), consistent with the tug-of-war identified in reanalysis. It should be noted that this analysis should be treated as a comparative case-study world rather than a predictive benchmark, also considering demonstrated temperature-humidity biases in models19,20.
Projected eCDD anomalies during hot extremes are significantly lower than in the present, indicating that for the same level of extreme heat (i.e., 95th percentile), the relative cooling-energy requirement is reduced compared to present-day conditions (Fig. 3c). Interestingly, differences in eCDD and CDD response during extremes are approximately the same to those found in reanalysis (i.e., Fig. 2d) for both present and future climates. This indicates that climate models can successfully capture the dry-heat versus humid-heat dichotomy over North America (Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9). In future projections, the central North America region of CDD overestimation (i.e., negative regions in Fig. 2d, and Supplementary Fig. 10) expands eastward, consistent with an increasing spatial extent of dry-heat extremes (Fig. 3d). However, central North America drying contrasts with the wetting trend observed in reanalysis, likely reflecting a common climate-model bias20. This error persists despite present and future simulations accurately reproducing the background SHR climatology (Supplementary Fig. 8a, b).
Power-grid vulnerability to cooling demand increases
Mapping projected changes in effective cooling demand onto the U.S. power grid using population-weighted estimates aggregated over major grid regions (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Emissions & Generation Resource Integrated Database (eGRID)) shows that the magnitude of future eCDD change varies widely, spanning nearly a fourfold range across the U.S. Increases are smallest in parts of the southeastern U.S., where eCDD rises by roughly 32.3%, and largest in the northeastern grid regions, where eCDD is projected to increase by 122.7% (Fig. 4a, b). Several regions in the Northwest, Great Lakes, and Mid-Atlantic also experience increases exceeding 100%. In contrast, some densely populated areas, such as the New York Long Island region (NYLI), exhibit large per-capita increases in eCDD that are partially offset by projected population declines, yielding a smaller net grid-scale increase than the neighboring New York City Westchester region (NYCW, i.e., +32.0%, see Supplementary Fig. 11).
Regions facing the largest projected increases in effective cooling demand tend to coincide with electricity systems that already rely less on fossil fuels and more on hydroelectric, nuclear, or other non-fossil sources (e.g., northeast and northwest U.S.; Fig. 4b, c). This association may partly arise from large-scale geographic structure, whereby northern grid regions most exposed to rising cooling demand often overlap with areas rich in hydropower along the eastern and western margins21, or with wind-dominated (but hydro-limited) systems across the central United States22. In contrast, projected eCDD growth is generally smaller in the southeastern U.S., where both hydropower and wind resources are comparatively limited (i.e., bottom right in Fig. 4c).
A notable exception occurs in grid regions west of the Great Lakes where increases in cooling demand are more likely to translate into additional fossil-fuel generation. These regions combine relatively large eCDD increases with limited low-carbon generation potential, owing to scarce hydropower, suboptimal wind resources, and northern latitudes that constrain solar output23. Importantly, these same regions are also those where conventional CDD more closely tracks eCDD, suggesting that earlier temperature-based analyses have likely captured future cooling demand growth reasonably well. Conversely, regions in southern central United States tend to exhibit smaller eCDD increases for their given emissions profile, often coinciding with abundant wind resources. Nonetheless, the observed inverse association between fossil-fuel share and projected eCDD change does not imply a causal relationship, i.e., that cleaner electricity systems reduce cooling-demand; rather, it reflects that regions facing the largest increases in cooling demand are, in many cases, already comparatively decarbonized.
Discussion
This study demonstrates that incorporating refrigeration thermodynamics and sensible-latent heat partitioning into cooling demand metrics fundamentally alters regional projections of energy needs. We introduce an efficiency-weighted cooling degree day (eCDD) metric, which accounts for temperature-dependent compressor performance and the humidity-sensitive fraction of cooling associated with sensible heat removal. Our results show that conventional temperature-only metrics, such as cooling degree days (CDD), miss important spatial and temporal patterns in efficiency-weighted cooling demand, particularly in regions where moisture trends alter the sensible-latent partitioning of cooling.
Historical data indicate that while cooling efficiency generally declines as temperatures rise, regional moisture trends can mitigate or exacerbate temperature-driven efficiency losses. As a result, eCDD anomalies during extreme heat events, and also their long term trends, can differ significantly from their corresponding CDD counterparts. Notably, during extreme heat events, humid extremes lower SHR and amplify efficiency losses, increasing the energy burden, while dry extremes raise SHR and can partially offset the penalties imposed by temperature. This humidity-dependence mirrors a broader recognition that co-occurring temperature and moisture anomalies can produce disproportionate impacts relative to either driver alone24. Recent extensions of the CDD framework have proposed wet-bulb temperature or enthalpy as the ambient forcing variable to better capture the full thermal burden on occupants9,25,26. Our results extend this logic to the mechanical side: humidity plays an equally critical role in governing cooling system efficiency, a compounding that no temperature- or wet-bulb-based metric alone can resolve.
Future climate projections show that effective cooling demand, as quantified here by eCDD, is expected to outpace the growth in temperature-driven demand, as captured by CDD, by 7.5–15.0% over much of the United States, while over 30% in areas in the far north. However, during hot extremes, the additional effective cooling demand is projected to be lower in the future for the same relative temperature anomaly, consistent with the tendency for relative humidity to decline on the hottest days under warming27, which raises SHR and partially offsets the compressor efficiency penalty. Efficiency dynamics mediated by both vapor-compression thermodynamics and humidity effects on SHR also introduce important regional structure that cannot be captured with simple temperature exceedance. Yet accurately characterizing this structure depends on climate models robustly reproducing the partitioning between dry and humid heat regimes, a known difficulty, as coarser-resolution models systematically misrepresent the moisture conditions associated with extreme heat20. Resolving this remains essential not only for human heat stress projections, but for accurate estimates of the mechanical cooling burden that depends on the same thermodynamic drivers28.
Aggregating effective cooling demand (eCDD) change at the grid level reveals spatial disparities in risk across the U.S. power system, with direct implications for demand forecasting, energy infrastructure planning, and climate adaptation. Regions with the largest projected increases in cooling demand tend to have lower shares of fossil-fuel generation. Treating CDD as a proxy for energy use introduces region- and state-dependent biases that can lead to misallocation of resources and misrepresentation of risk, particularly in regions where efficiency changes are greatest. By accounting for temperature-dependent compressor performance and SHR-linked moisture effects, eCDD provides a thermodynamically-informed basis for comparing regional efficiency-weighted cooling demand and for integrating demand projections with supply-side constraints (e.g., energy mix and infrastructure) and mitigation strategies. However, eCDD should be interpreted as an efficiency-weighted CDD proxy, rather than a complete estimate of total cooling load, because it captures temperature-dependent compressor performance and sensible–latent partitioning but does not represent all building-, system-, and behavior-specific drivers of cooling demand.
While this study employs a simplified refrigeration model, the framework is intended as an initial step to move beyond temperature-only CDD, demonstrating how explicitly accounting for efficiency is essential for diagnosing regional differences in efficiency-weighted cooling demand and for articulating the climatic requirements that future cooling technologies must meet. Future work should seek to integrate eCDD with detailed building and grid simulations (e.g., building energy models and management systems), and should account for evolving technologies and standards (e.g., alternative refrigerants, dehumidification, and more physically detailed system representations). Future work should also seek to combine the efficiency-weighting approach developed here with emerging efforts to improve the demand side of CDD itself, including wet-bulb-, enthalpy-, or psychrometric-load-based exposure metrics, thereby accounting for both the climatic drivers of cooling load and the efficiency with which that load is met. Furthermore, we focus primarily on long-term trends and extremes, while interannual variability is reserved for future investigation. Uncertainties in climate projections remain an area of concern, particularly regarding humidity trends and land-atmosphere interactions, as noted above. For example, model-derived humidity diagnostics may be indirectly affected by known biases in land-surface evapotranspiration partitioning over North America, which could potentially alter relative humidity as well as the demarcation between regions where humid-heat or dry-heat events occur29.
In summary, an efficiency-aware cooling degree day metric, eCDD, is important for projecting future efficiency-weighted cooling demand in regions where temperature and humidity co-evolve. This work presents a framework connecting climate and the thermodynamic principles of refrigeration, clearly demonstrating where the implicit assumptions underlying cooling degree days fall short. Viewed through this lens, cooling efficiency is governed by climate, not merely engineered into machines.
Methods
Climate data
This study uses hourly 2-meter temperature (t2m) and 2-meter dew point (d2m) data from the Fifth-Generation European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) global atmospheric reanalysis (ERA5). The time periods assessed is from January 1, 1971, to December 31, 202030, and ERA5 data is provided on a regular 0.25∘ × 0.25∘ latitude-longitude grid. Future projections are derived from a 19 multi-model ensemble from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6, see Table 1) using daily data. Experimental forcing use the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP)5-8.5 emissions scenario (high forcing) for future runs, while the present experiment represents the forced atmosphere run for 1950-2014. To ensure equal temporal coverage, only the final 36 years (1979-2014) of the historical period are used, matching the 36-year duration of the future experiment.

Idealized refrigeration model
We create an idealized refrigeration model to capture the thermodynamic dependence of cooling efficiency on environmental conditions and use a single refrigerant, R134a, as a representative example of how efficiency responds to changes in the climate. The model calculates the change in enthalpy (h) between the four principal stages of the vapor-compression cycle (h1, h2, h3, h4). In this framework, h1 → h2 represents isentropic compression, h2 → h3 condensation at high pressure, h3 → h4 isenthalpic expansion, and h4 → h1 evaporation at low pressure.
Several key assumptions are applied in these calculations. First, the evaporator temperature is fixed at 0∘C, which provides a midpoint between typical operating conditions for refrigerators (−50 to −25∘C)31 and air conditioners (approximately 6.85∘C)32. This choice establishes an idealized baseline for comparing system performance without biasing the analysis toward either application type, while avoiding effects associated with sub-freezing evaporator temperatures (e.g., frost accumulation, reduced effective heat exchange). Second, we assume an isentropic efficiency of 0.8 as a representative mid-range value33. Finally, we assume a constant temperature difference (TΔ) of 10∘C between the condenser temperature and outside ambient temperature34. We adopt this idealized thermodynamics-based formulation rather than the Carnot COP approximation (i.e., perfectly reversible refrigeration cycle) to provide a more realistic representation of refrigeration performance and to allow for flexibility in specifying different model parameters and refrigerant types13. Finally, the model does not account for additional processes, such as superheating or subcooling.
To account for humidity’s influence on cooling efficiency, we extend the coefficient of performance to an effective coefficient of performance (eCOP) by incorporating the sensible heat ratio (SHR). The SHR represents the fraction of the total cooling load that is due to sensible heat removal (temperature reduction) relative to the combined sensible and latent components, as defined in equation (4):

This prevents unphysical negative latent heat values that would otherwise imply condensation occurring in reverse (moisture addition), which does not contribute to cooling.

In this formulation, COP captures the temperature-dependent performance of the vapor-compression cycle, while SHR captures the fraction of total cooling delivered as sensible cooling. The eCOP therefore reflects two distinct effects: the reduction in compressor performance under higher temperature lift, and the reduction in useful sensible cooling when part of the cooling load is diverted toward latent moisture removal. Together, these terms ensure that eCOP reflects a more realistic measure of system efficiency under varying thermal and moisture conditions.
Index definitions and diagnostics
The cooling degree days (CDD) index is calculated relative to a threshold of 18 ∘C, as given in below equation:
| | 9 |
where Tamb,i is the hourly t2m. Leap-day data (February 29) are removed to maintain consistent year lengths across the record. The index is presented in degree-hours, and normalization by the constant factor of 24 to convert to degree-days was omitted, as it does not affect the derived relative measures (percentage change, z-scores, etc.) central to this analysis. Conversion to degree-days can be achieved by dividing by 24. We chose 18 ∘C threshold (Tthresh), as this was the most commonly used value across disciplines, including climate science8, futures markets36, and energy demand analysis37.
To incorporate the thermodynamic efficiency of cooling systems into cooling degree days, we define an effective cooling degree day (eCDD) index. The eCDD index is therefore expressed as:
| | 10 |
As CMIP6 fields are daily rather than hourly resolution, we approximate cooling degree days using the UK Met Office method38 which uses the minimum, maximum, and mean daily temperature to approximate the diurnal cycle. To validate this approximation, we compared daily estimates with values computed directly from hourly data and found close agreement for temperature, efficiency, and eCDD metrics on days exceeding the 18∘C cooling threshold (see Supplementary Fig. 12).
Extreme-temperature analyses for both the historical reanalysis and CMIP6 projections follow a consistent procedure. First, we remove February 29 from all datasets to obtain a uniform 365-day calendar. At each grid point, we then detrend daily temperature and all other diagnostic fields using a linear least-squares fit over the full analysis period (1971–2020 for ERA5; 1979–2014 and 2015–2050 for the CMIP present and future segments, respectively). From the detrended fields, we construct a day-of-year climatology and corresponding standard deviation for each calendar day by averaging over all available years. Daily standardized anomalies (z-scores) are then computed as the detrended anomaly divided by the day-of-year standard deviation at each grid point. Hot extremes are defined on a pointwise basis as all days between May and September (MJJAS) for which the t2m z-score exceeds +1.645 (95th percentile). Composites for each field (e.g., SHR, eCOP, eCDD) are formed by averaging the corresponding standardized anomalies over all hot days at each latitude and longitude location, such that the number of contributing events varies spatially according to the local frequency of extremes. For the CMIP analyses, the standardization (climatology and variance) is performed separately for the present and future periods, ensuring that z-scores and composites are defined relative to each period’s own internal variability.
Statistical significance is assessed using a nonparametric bootstrap with 1000 resamples, drawn with replacement. For each bootstrap iteration, n years are randomly selected, where n is the length of the given sample, and resampling is applied on a point-wise basis (i.e., at each latitude-longitude grid cell). Confidence intervals are determined from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. A signal is considered significant at the 95% level if the interval excludes zero (i.e., upper < 0 or lower > 0). The null hypothesis for the slope analyses is that the trend equals zero, and resampling is performed from the entire record. Field significance was additionally assessed following the approach of Wilks39 using a false discovery rate approach with an alpha of 0.1 to account for multiple testing across spatially correlated grid cells.
To assess the relative effect of including COP, we paired each pointwise eCDD slope with the corresponding CDD slope and computed the error slope field, as given in below equation:
| | 11 |
To assess whether the CDD and eCDD trends were significantly different, we performed a paired bootstrap with 1000 resamples, recomputing both indices’ slopes simultaneously using the same random years. The distribution of slope differences provided 95% bootstrap percentile intervals, and grid cells where these intervals excluded zero were classified as regions where the CDD and eCDD trends differ significantly. To account for spatially correlated grid cells, we additionally assessed field significance with an alpha of 0.1 following approach of Wilks39, ensuring that mapped trends are interpreted only where the spatial pattern exceeds what would be expected by chance.
Finally, to compute spatial averages of energy grids, we use the U.S. EPA’s eGRID 2023 subregion boundaries. For simple regional means (e.g., area-averaged CDD or eCDD trends), grid cells are weighted by the cosine of latitude to approximate their relative surface area. To quantify changes in population-weighted cooling demand, we instead combine eCDD with gridded population datasets. For the historical period (1979-2014), we use year 2000 population counts from the Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (GPWv440) Population Count product, which provides a temporal midpoint. For the future period (2015-2050), we use year 2030 population projections from the Global One-Eighth Degree Urban Land Extent Projection and Base Year Grids under the SSP5 demographic projections41. Where these fields are provided as densities (persons km−2), they are converted to counts by multiplying by the corresponding grid-cell area inferred from the spherical grid geometry.
Population-weighted eCDD is then constructed on a grid-cell basis as the product of population and period-mean eCDD and summed within each eGRID region. The fractional change in population-weighted eCDD between the future and present periods is then expressed as:

where Pp and Pf are the present- and future-period populations, and eCDDp and eCDDf are the corresponding period-mean eCDD values.

Brookfield and CDPQ acquire Antylia Scientific from GTCR for US$1.34 billion
On May 28, 2025, Brookfield Asset Management’s private equity arm and CDPQ have jointly acquired Antylia Scientific from GTCR in a transaction valued at approximately US$1.34 billion (C$1.83 billion at the time of the announcement). Headquartered in Vernon Hills, Illinois, Antylia is a diversified life sciences company serving the biopharmaceutical, clinical diagnostic, and environmental testing industries with critical laboratory products. The sale marks a major milestone in GTCR’s decade-long stewardship of Antylia, originally acquired in 2014 in a carve-out from Thermo Fisher Scientific under GTCR’s Leaders Strategy™. Over the years, GTCR partnered with Antylia Chairman Bernd Brust and CEO Jonathan Salkin to drive transformational growth through significant capital investments and 15 strategic add-on acquisitions. Notably, in 2021, Antylia divested its Masterflex bioprocessing segment to Avantor Inc. for US$2.9 billion, further refining its core focus areas. The transaction underscores Antylia's evolution into a key platform in life sciences tools and quality controls.
Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP advised Brookfield Asset Management’ in this transaction, while Mayer Brown advised CDPQ. Goldman Sachs and Jefferies served as financial advisors to Antylia, with Kirkland & Ellis providing legal counsel. J.P. Morgan Securities LLC advised GTCR.

FBI’s IC3 Finds Almost $8.5 Billion Lost to Business Email Compromise in Last Three Years
It’s a figure even the FBI called “staggering”: The losses reported to its Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) in 2024 totaled $16.6 billion, the bulk of which came from fraud. And among those frauds, business email compromise (BEC) remained a pervasive threat.
In the IC3 2024 Annual Report, released April 23, officials found that BEC was the 7th most reported crime to IC3 last year, with 21,442 complaints. However, BEC was second on the dollar list, with close to $2.8 billion in losses.
While both numbers remained fairly consistent in recent years—there were just 47 fewer BEC reports last year compared to 2023—the financial damage is stark, with nearly $8.5 billion in BEC losses reported to IC3 between 2022 and 2024.
IC3’s report came barely a week after the Association for Financial Professionals (AFP) released its 2025 Fraud and Control Survey Report, which found that 63% of organizations experienced BEC last year. AFP and said “BEC remains a significant threat.”
Changes to the Nacha Rules are taking effect in 2026, aimed at reducing the incidence of successful fraud attempts through tactics such as BEC, and improving the recovery of funds after frauds have occurred.
Overall, IC3 received nearly 860,000 complaints last year. Phishing/spoofing was the most reported type of crime with 193,407. Ransomware came in at No. 20, with 3,156 complaints, but B. Chad Yarbrough, the FBI’s Operations Director for Criminal and Cyber, called it “the most pervasive threat to critical infrastructure.”
The IC3 report also noted that cyber-enabled fraud—where criminals use the internet or other technology to commit fraud—was responsible for almost 83% of all losses reported to IC3 last year, $13.7 billion. That included an increasingly popular scam: demanding money for supposedly unpaid tolls, which had more than 59,000 complaints.
“During its infancy, IC3 received roughly 2,000 complaints every month. For the past five years, IC3 has averaged more than 2,000 complaints every day,” Yarbrough wrote in his introduction to the report.
