Narrative: Frontline already has what took Smith + Howard 3.5 years to build (national reach, offshore delivery, about half the AM Law 200), so its plan is to earn more per firm, move down-market and go international. At close it had roughly $100-140M of revenue and $16-20M of adjusted EBITDA (est.), bought at about 12-15x with $137M+ of equity and a $90M NXT/Audax term loan, so EBITDA growth has to carry the return. Phase 1 (months 0-12) turns HELIX into a product-led service desk with a Tier-0 AI agent, then adds a cyber-posture subscription and legal-AI enablement for the AM Law base, where ILTA finds 68% of firms have Copilot but only 8% have deployed it firm-wide. Phase 2 (months 6-18) goes after the 143 mid-size firms (17,042 attorneys) in our 16-metro screen, 37 of which score 65+, and buys local legal MSPs such as Kraft Kennedy, Tabush, Innovative Computing Systems and PSM Partners, just as Smith + Howard opened with Market Street Partners. Phase 3 (months 12-30) consolidates eBilling and AR now that client-side AI has pushed invoice rejections from 11% to 18%, buying from a screen that includes Helm360, The Garver Group and The Legal Billing Group and running four finance agents priced on days-to-pay. Phase 4 (months 24-42) builds the UK and Canada through acquired local providers (Quiss, Accurate Legal Billing, CG Technologies), the way Consilio entered the UK through Lawyers On Demand, because Frontline's own London subsidiary booked only about GBP 0.6M in 2024. The single Smith + Howard move most worth copying is Geels Norton: a SOC 2 and ISO cyber-assurance capability bought months before TPG signed, which Frontline should own before any sale process. On talent, the Hyderabad, Goa and Cape Town base needs a named leader with an integration mandate, as the S+H India team got, plus a certification ladder and a US apprenticeship track. The KPI roadmap is an explicit assumption rather than guidance: revenue moves from about $130M to $215M and EBITDA from $20M to $41M over 36 months, with about $55M of acquired revenue and margin rising from roughly 15% to 19%. Funding is the binding constraint, since incremental debt at sector-norm leverage covers perhaps $15-35M against a $50-80M add-on plan, so a co-invest top-up should be planned now. The diligence gaps to close first are the 300-versus-900 client count, actual churn and recurring mix, and the undisclosed revolver or delayed-draw facility, and the KL Software deal (Aug 2026) should be recorded as a partnership rather than an acquisition.

Generated: 2026-09-24
Method: SEC EDGAR full-text search (efts.sec.gov) and submissions API for Form D, N-PORT, N-CSR and BDC 10-K/10-Q schedules; direct parsing of Form D XML and N-PORT XML; UK Companies House public web pages (filing history, officers, charges) with accounts PDFs rendered locally and read page by page; SBA PPP FOIA PPP loans over $150k CSV scanned locally; company press releases and About page (frontlinems.com); BSP news page. WebSearch budget was exhausted, so discovery relied on direct registries and EDGAR. ProPublica, FederalPay and OpenCorporates were blocked by bot challenges and were not bypassed.
Sources summary: SEC EDGAR (BSP-FL LP and BSP-FL Co-Invest Form Ds; Broad Sky Partners LP Form D/As; other BSP deal-vehicle Form Ds; Carlyle AlpInvest Private Markets Fund N-PORT-P x5 and N-CSR; Audax Credit BDC, Audax Private Credit Fund, Golub Capital Direct Lending, WhiteHorse Finance and Runway Growth 10-K/10-Q schedules); UK Companies House (Intelliteach Ltd 07039190 accounts FY2022-FY2024, officers, charges); SBA PPP FOIA; frontlinems.com (About, Awards, Press, Leadership, press releases 2020-2026); broadskypartners.com/news.
Caveats:
- The $90M term-loan figure comes from UK subsidiary notes describing the group facility. Revolver, DDTL or incremental tranches since Dec 2024 are not disclosed.
- Whether Carlyle AlpInvest's $12.5M in BSP-FL Intermediate Inc. is additional to, or part of, the $137M BSP-FL LP raise is unknown, so total equity is given as a range.
- EBITDA, revenue and EV figures are analyst estimates from leverage and multiple assumptions, not disclosed financials.
- The client count varies by source: 800+ (Dec 2024), 900+ (2025-26) and '300 Law Firms Served' on the current homepage. Scope definitions likely differ.
- Mapping BSP vehicle codes (TS, BPI, CET) to portfolio companies is inferred from press timing.
- UK accounts omit the P&L (small-companies regime), but the FY2024 accounts include a turnover note: GBP 581,072 (2024) and GBP 728,131 (2023).
- Verified 2026-09-24: sampled 21, confirmed 21, removed 0
Financial picture: Frontline was bought by BSP on Dec 9, 2024 through BSP-FL Holdings Inc. The deal was funded by an equity vehicle (BSP-FL LP) that sold $136.95M to 21 investors, plus a $90M initial term loan co-led by NXT Capital and Audax Private Debt (UK sub accounts, note 11). Carlyle AlpInvest separately put $12.5M of equity directly into BSP-FL Intermediate Inc. on Dec 5, 2024, and BV Investment Partners rolled a minority stake. Sponsor equity is therefore roughly $137-150M plus rollover, against $90M of debt, or about 60% equity. Adding equity and debt gives a transaction value of roughly $230-260M. If the lenders sized the $90M loan at a typical 4.5-5.5x LMM leverage, adjusted EBITDA at close was about $16-20M, for an entry multiple of about 12-15x. The BV-era debt history supports that range. Webster Bank lent $30M plus a $5M revolver in Feb 2019, and term debt reached $47.7M by Dec 2023 after the 2020-21 add-ons. At bank-style 3-4x leverage, that implies 2023 EBITDA of about $12-16M, growing into the $16-20M implied at the BSP close. Headcount rose from 600+ (2020, after Hilltop) to about 850 (c.2022), 1,000+ (2023) and about 1,100 (Jan 2026), with a heavy offshore base (Goa, Hyderabad, Cape Town). At an assumed $90-130K revenue per employee for an offshore-weighted legal MSP/BPO, revenue is estimated at about $100-140M, implying 13-18% EBITDA margins. The MSP 501 ranks (#38 in 2024, #36 in 2026) weight revenue, EBITDA and recurring revenue, which supports a large-MSP scale ($100M+) without giving an exact band. After the close, Carlyle held the position at cost for five quarters, then marked it up about 10% to $13.75M at 3/31/2026, a modest positive signal after the Jan 2026 CEO change to Tim Britt (ex-Synoptek roll-up founder). Relative to rivals, Frontline's structure is simpler and cheaper than Elevate's (about 12.8%+ venture debt), less stretched than Consilio's (senior plus PIK sub debt), and healthier-looking than Epiq's (loan marked about 91% of par). Frontline's own loan pricing is not public, but Audax's comparable LMM unitranches (for example Mitratech at S+475) suggest roughly S+475-550. Main open risks: undisclosed incremental debt for a likely buy-and-build (KL Software, Aug 2026), UK sub filing lapses, and inconsistent client-count disclosures.

Landscape summary:
- Fund I is about $335M (Form D), one of the smallest on this map; rivals for similar deals run $0.9-2.1B flagships (Trivest VII $950M, Bertram V $1.5B, Gridiron V $2.1B). BSP's $50-250M equity checks therefore lean on co-invest and operating credibility.
- The closest thesis-level peers are firms that are pure business-services or services-plus-consumer shops in a similar equity band: MidOcean (Zachem's former firm, same sector taxonomy including franchise services and media/marketing), CIVC (business-services only; legal support, IT, utility services), Trilantic North America ($50-300M checks, business services + consumer), Palladium ($50-150M), Vesterra/Comvest (up to $150M) and Bertram ($150-500M EV).
- Residential services (Punctual Pros) is the most crowded field. National consolidators (Apex/Alpine, Wrench/LGP, TurnPoint/OMERS, Redwood/Altas, Any Hour/Knox Lane, T3/Riverside) set add-on pricing. In PA/NJ specifically, Sila (Goldman Sachs), Legacy Service Partners/HL Bowman (Gridiron), Ally Services (Watchtower) and Northwinds (TruArc) are buying in or next to Punctual Pros' counties.
- Commercial electrical and energy services (CET) have only recently drawn institutional money. Cascade Partners reports that PE now accounts for most electrical-contractor M&A since 2023, with new companies from Kohlberg (RESA Power, Loenbro, plus CLEAResult in energy efficiency) and Huron (Criticore; Albireo Energy expanding into Upstate NY). CET is still one of very few sponsor-backed electrical companies anchored in New England.
- Legal services (Frontline) have a thin set of sponsor competitors: Stone Point/Aquiline's Consilio (eDiscovery/review), EagleTree's Integreon (legal managed services; ownership may have changed), CIVC's Magna Legal Services, Gridiron's Esquire Deposition Solutions, and BV Investment Partners (Frontline's former owner). None of them combines law-firm IT managed services with billing/RCM the way Frontline does.
- Lab supply distribution (Thomas Scientific) has one very aggressive sponsor-backed consolidator, StoneCalibre's Calibre Scientific, which made more than a dozen lab distribution and consumables acquisitions in 2024 alone, mostly in Europe; its U.S. diagnostics foothold (Alpha-Tec) dates to 2017. Sterling's distribution mandate (consumables/MRO) is the other relevant overlap.
- Public affairs and communications (BPI) turned over sponsor-to-sponsor in 2025 when Shamrock Capital bought Penta Group from Falfurrias. Most other institutional money in PR sits with large caps (KKR/FGS Global) or holding companies (Stagwell), which leaves mid-market ownership of public-affairs firms uncrowded.
- Consumer apparel (Fair Harbor) has the least verified overlap in this research. Only generalist consumer investors (Bertram, Palladium, Trilantic, EagleTree, Gryphon) appear, and no dedicated apparel sponsor was profiled, so the competitive picture there is incomplete.
- Upmarket sponsors (Leonard Green, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Court Square, Audax, Stone Point, Altas) matter mainly as exit buyers. Recent sponsor-to-sponsor trades (NEFCO Bertram to LGP, Service Logic LGP to Bain, Sila MSCP to GS, Jensen Hughes Gryphon to New Mountain, Smith + Howard BSP to TPG Growth) show deep demand for scaled services companies.
Sector heatmap:
Punctual pros:

Most active:
gs_sila; gridiron; watchtower; truarc; alpine; knox_lane; altas_redwood; omers_pe; leonard_green; riverside; trivest
Intensity: very high
Note: Sila (ECS Comfort in Lebanon/Dauphin/Lancaster) and Legacy/HL Bowman (Harrisburg/York/Lancaster/Reading) sit inside Punctual Pros' core counties, and Ally Services covers PA and NJ.
Cet:
Sector: Commercial electrical, solar/EV, energy efficiency, wastewater electrical (New England)
Most active:
kohlberg; huron; sterling; tailwind; civc; court_square; vesterra_comvest; midocean
Intensity: medium, rising
Note: New electrical/energy roll-ups (Kohlberg's RESA Power, Loenbro and CLEAResult; Huron's Criticore and Albireo) are mostly outside New England today; Albireo's Upstate NY move is the nearest.
Frontline:
Sector: Legal IT managed services + law-firm billing/RCM
Most active:
stone_point; eagletree; civc; gridiron; bv_investment; alpine; renovus
Intensity: low-medium
Note: Sponsors own eDiscovery, managed review, court reporting and generalist MSP roll-ups (Alpine's Evergreen), but no verified sponsor-backed company combines legal IT and RCM.
Thomas scientific:
Sector: Lab supplies, equipment & supply-chain distribution
Most active:

Note: Calibre Scientific is the main competitor for chromatography/consumables/glassware add-ons.

Intensity: low-medium
Note: Shamrock/Penta (Aug 2025) is the key mid-market comparable; MidOcean's media & marketing theme is the Zachem-lineage overlap.

Most active:

Intensity: low (insufficient data)
Note: No dedicated apparel sponsor was verified in this pass.
Implications for bsp:
- Punctual Pros faces the hardest add-on competition. Sila (Goldman Sachs), Legacy/HL Bowman (Gridiron) and Ally (Watchtower) are all buying in Central PA/NJ. BSP should lean on the franchise-system angle (Authority Brands territory rights, brand conversion) and on proprietary outreach to sub-$3M EBITDA shops that large-cap sponsors skip, rather than join auctions.
- CET has open space in New England. Institutional electrical/energy roll-ups (Kohlberg's RESA Power, Loenbro and CLEAResult; Huron's Criticore and Albireo) are mostly outside the six-state footprint, so CET can keep consolidating New England electrical, wastewater and energy-efficiency contractors (Horton-style) before those roll-ups reach the region. Albireo's Upstate NY expansion and Kohlberg's energy-efficiency cluster are the ones to watch.
- Frontline's legal IT + RCM combination has no direct sponsor-backed copy. The likely challengers are Alpine's Evergreen (MSP roll-up), EagleTree/Integreon and BV (the former owner), so BSP should lock in law-firm MSP and billing-services add-ons before a generalist MSP consolidator builds a legal vertical.
- Thomas Scientific should treat Calibre Scientific as its main bidding competitor for U.S. chromatography, consumables and specialty-distribution add-ons, and could use Calibre's European focus to win U.S. line-card and distribution targets.
- At the fund level, MidOcean, CIVC, Trilantic NA, Palladium and Vesterra run the same business-services/consumer approach with larger pools. The Smith + Howard exit to TPG Growth (about 100 to 800 professionals, 9 add-ons) is BSP's best proof point for Fund II fundraising and for winning founder-led deals on operating credibility. Upmarket buyers (LGP, GS, Court Square, New Mountain, Bain, TPG) are clearly paying for scaled services companies, which supports exit multiples.
Excluded candidates:
- Firm: LLR Partners
Reason: LLR VII ($2.45B, Apr 2025) focuses on technology and healthcare; business services not a stated focus.
Source url: https://www.llrpartners.com/llr-closes-seventh-fund-at-2-45-billion/
- Firm: Corridor Capital (Heartland Home Services)
Reason: Heartland Home Services is owned by The Jordan Company with Cobepa (minority), not Corridor. Corridor's contractor-adjacent deal (CEO Warrior) is a training business, not a competing company.
Source url: https://www.rwbaird.com/transactions/investment-banking/dealcard/5650/
- Firm: Waud Capital Partners
Reason: Current website lists only healthcare and software & technology sectors.
Source url: https://www.waudcapital.com/
- Firm: Boathouse Capital
Reason: Focused on SaaS/software, tech-enabled services and healthcare IT with small checks ($300M Fund III); no overlap with BSP portfolio companies.
Source url: https://boathousecapital.com/boathouse-capital-successfully-closes-oversubscribed-300-million-fund-iii/
- Firm: PSG
Reason: Listed as 'only if fit'; software-growth investor. Not researched further and no overlap found.
- Firm: Huron Capital / Sciens Building Solutions
Reason: Kept as Huron Capital, but Sciens itself was sold to Carlyle in Dec 2021 and is treated as exited.
Source url: https://www.huroncapital.com/news/huron-capital-completes-the-sale-of-sciens-building-solutions/
Caveats:
- Web search quota ran out partway through research, so later firms were verified mainly from firm websites and previously retrieved search results. Some fund sizes (Gryphon VI, Trilantic VII, Palladium VI, Tailwind IV, Shore Business Services II) are unknown and set to null.
- Several Business Wire pages returned HTTP 403. Where cited, those URLs come from search results rather than fetched pages.
- 2025-2026 deals covers disclosed transactions only; many sponsors do not announce add-ons, so counts are lower bounds. Some entries record partial liquidity (e.g., Apollo's minority stake in Apex) or structured-equity deals typed as an exit or an initial buyout with explanatory notes.
- Add-on counts in the relevant-companies lists mix lifetime and single-year figures (see notes); treat them as indicative.
- AUM figures come from different dates (e.g., Shore about $17B on its website vs. $14B+ in Oct 2025; Kohlberg about $15B in 2024 vs. $18B on its website).
- HQ coordinates are city centroids (location precision: city). HQs for Huron (Detroit), Stone Point (Greenwich), Trilantic NA (New York), Sverica (Boston), Alpine (San Francisco) and OMERS (Toronto) come from general knowledge and were not confirmed on a fetched page.
- Threat levels and implications are analyst judgments, not reported facts.
- Smith + Howard is excluded as a BSP overlap sector because it was sold (TPG Growth, closed Aug 6, 2026).
- Integreon: the Global Legal Post 'Law.com's owner' headline describes EagleTree's own Jun 2021 purchase (EagleTree owns ALM); no later sale found.
- CIVC Fund VII ($870M, 2023) could not be confirmed on a fetched page (PitchBook blocked); civc.com confirms 7 funds and $2B invested.
- Verified 2026-09-24: sampled 35, confirmed 34, removed 0

Audience: Storm/cold-snap zone homeowners in Tier-I zips; triggered 12-36 h before NWS Extreme Cold or Winter Storm warnings
Hook: Your furnace doesn't know a storm is coming. We do.
Script:
- T sec: 0
Visual: Night exterior, Central PA farmhouse-style home, snow starting under a porch light; radar sweep overlay
Voiceover: Your furnace doesn't know a storm is coming.
On screen text: Winter Storm Warning tonight
- T sec: 4
Visual: Branded van pulling into a lit driveway at dusk, tech checking a tablet with a dispatch map
Voiceover: We do. Our techs are staged before it hits.
On screen text: Crews pre-positioned
- T sec: 9
Visual: Warm living room, family on sofa, thermostat reading 70
Voiceover: One Hour Heating & Air Conditioning. Always On Time... Or You Don't Pay A Dime!
On screen text: Always On Time... Or You Don't Pay A Dime!®
- T sec: 13
Visual: End card: logo, QR, tracking number, 'Service-call fee waived if late. Details at onehourheatandair.com/southeast-pa'
On screen text: Book now - scan or call
Cta: Scan the QR or call to book a no-heat visit before the storm
Offer: Priority booking for members; illustrative non-member offer: service-call fee waived for online bookings during the warning window (confirm with PP price book)
Brand rules:
Brand: One Hour Heating & Air Conditioning®
Promise exact: Always On Time... Or You Don't Pay A Dime!®
Promise terms: Technician arrives within the customer-selected window or the service call is free (SE PA guarantees page). Also: 100% Satisfaction Guarantee on materials, labor and craftsmanship up to two years; StraightForward Pricing®.
Do:
Use the full registered name on first mention and on the end card; Quote the promise verbatim with ®; Super 'Service-call fee waived if late; see onehourheatandair.com/southeast-pa for details' when the promise is spoken
Dont:
Paraphrase to 'on time or it's free' (it is the service call, not the repair); Imply 24/7 or same-day unless the location offers it

Method: CTV platform terms, benchmarks and franchisor brand promises were fetched from the cited pages on 2026-10-06 (WebFetch/curl); where a page returned 403 or was gated, the figure comes from the search-engine result for that URL and the item is marked retrieval status='search snippet'. Territory facts were computed from repo data: Punctual Pros ZIP coverage (248 flagged zips, 1,001,408 housing units, 61 Tier-I zips with 336,002 units), data/sales deed feeds (trailing-12-month arm's-length residential sales by county; 33% of Lancaster/York/Cumberland/Dauphin residential sales are pre-1980 homes), Punctual Pros storm-event history (NOAA monthly event counts) and the Punctual Pros demand model (NWS weather-response plans). Media plans are computed in code from the benchmark items with explicit formulas in each plan's 'model' field; every output is an estimate. Creative is original sample copy written to each brand's published guarantee language.

Notes: Dauphin (85 sales) and Franklin (0 in trailing 12 months) are under-counted in the deed feed, so 2,300/month is a floor-adjusted estimate (~24.9k counted + ~3k gap)/12.
Caveats:
- No public home-services CTV cost-per-site-visit or CPL benchmark was found; the $12 cost per visit is an assumption anchored on DTC case studies and must be replaced by the week-8 read.
- Mail lead rate (1.0% per piece) is deliberately below ANA prospect response (4-5%) and vendor new-mover claims (4.9%); treat both as upper bounds.
- SearchLight and LocaliQ disagree on search CPL ($104 blended Jan 2026 vs $128 HVAC Apr 2024-Mar 2025) because of different samples and lead definitions; plans use SearchLight because it also reports book rates and closed revenue.
- Mister Sparky's national guarantee ('the repair is free') differs from the Lancaster location page ('we'll pay you back'); creative uses the safe line until PP confirms.
- All offers are illustrative; prices, discounts and membership terms must come from PP's price book and Authority Brands' marketing standards. Multi-brand ads need franchisor approval (assumption about franchise agreement terms).

Strategy summary: Punctual Pros' three franchise brands all promise punctuality, so the ads should sell that promise (One Hour's 'Always On Time... Or You Don't Pay A Dime!', Ben Franklin's $5-a-minute guarantee, Mister Sparky's 'America's On-Time Electrician') rather than invent new claims. Google Local Services Ads are the cheapest high-intent leads in the category ($39-57 per lead at a ~44% book rate, SearchLight Feb 2026), so LSA is the always-on base and is managed through reviews and fast answer rates rather than bids. Self-serve CTV has dropped to $50-$500 minimums and roughly $15-40 CPMs with zip targeting (Vibe, Disney Campaign Manager, Universal Ads, YouTube on TV screens), which lets a ~$22M franchisee buy TV in its ~240 zips without paying for the whole Harrisburg or Philadelphia DMA. CTV's job is to make the brand familiar before the furnace fails and to lift branded search and LSA conversion, so it is judged on cost per booked job and geo-holdout lift, not completion rate (which is ~94-99% by construction). New-mover direct mail is the highest-intent prospect list a home-services company can get: county deed records show ~2,300 arm's-length residential sales a month in the PA core and ~1,150 on the Jersey Shore, each a household that must pick an HVAC, plumbing and electrical provider within months. One in three of those PA buyers bought a pre-1980 home, which drives the Ben Franklin and Mister Sparky older-home inspection offers and the CTV zip weighting toward older housing stock (Punctual Pros ZIP coverage older-housing share). The weather index ties it together: NWS alerts for PP's zones (the demand model's weather-response plans) trigger budget multipliers and creative swaps 12-36 hours before demand spikes, so spend lands when calls are about to rise rather than after phones are already full. The same deed feed becomes the CTV and Meta audience (address-matched households) and the mail list, so one new mover sees a coordinated welcome across mailbox, TV and phone, measured against a random holdout. Test first with an 8-week, $50k/month Central PA pilot: LSA profile and review clean-up, a zip-level CTV geo holdout in the 61 Tier-I zips, and a mail-versus-holdout new-mover drip, all on unique call-tracking numbers in ServiceTitan. If measured cost per booked job beats the modelled ~$185-200 blended, scale to the Jersey Shore (zip-only CTV) and then a regional Mid-Atlantic program, which also leaves a documented, attributed customer-acquisition engine for the exit data room.

title: Punctual Pros demand model: records

text:
Weather-to-service-call elasticities and storm response plans

Generated: 2026-09-24
Method: Baselines are derived from national homeowner surveys (American Home Shield 2024 share of homeowners calling each trade; Census American Housing Survey breakdown incidence; DuraPlas maintenance survey) converted to calls/day per 10k households with stated visit-frequency assumptions. Weather multipliers use ServiceTitan heat-wave elasticities (+20% calls, +25% jobs, +55–90% revenue) and NWS/Consumer Reports thresholds; magnitudes without a public elasticity are labeled "assumption" with rationale. Local exceedance frequencies were computed from NOAA GHCN-Daily (2019–2025) for hub stations, event-history counts from NOAA Storm Events, and zone/UGC codes and hub grid metadata were pulled live from api.weather.gov.
Formula:
Expected calls[trade,county,day]: baseline calls per 10k households (by trade) x households (by county)/10,000 x monthly index (by trade and month) x max(weather multipliers active for trade that day, with 0.5 x each additional independent driver above 1.0) x housing-age modifier
Pp expected calls: expected calls x Punctual Pros market share (by county) (parameter; set from PP booked-call history / ServiceTitan data)
Combination rule basis: assumption — avoids double counting correlated drivers (e.g., heat + humidity)
Multiplier point estimate: use midpoint of range until calibrated
Calibration: Regress PP daily booked calls by trade on TMAX/TMIN/PRCP/WSF5 from the hub stations (GHCN-Daily) and NWS alert flags; replace assumption ranges with fitted elasticities once 12+ months of PP data are loaded.
Sources summary:
ServiceTitan (heat-wave study; State of the Trades after-hours data); Samsara HVAC service-trip telematics; American Home Shield homeowner survey (Nov 2024); US Census Bureau American Housing Survey brief (1999); ACHR News (DuraPlas maintenance survey; service agreements); Housecall Pro 2026 Home Services Report; Consumer Reports (frozen pipe threshold); Insurance Information Institute (lightning claims 2025); Climate Central (weather-related outages 2000–2023); National Weather Service (weather.gov product definitions, LWX criteria, api.weather.gov zones/points/alert types); NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily and Storm Events; Nature Communications 2026 (effective CDD); OpenStreetMap Nominatim (hub geocoding)
Nws product naming note: api.weather.gov/alerts/types (retrieved 2026-09-24) lists "Extreme Heat Warning/Watch" and "Extreme Cold Warning/Watch" and "Cold Weather Advisory"; the legacy names Excessive Heat Warning and Wind Chill Warning/Advisory no longer appear — portal filters should match both names for historical alerts.
Caveats:
- No public source gives calls per 10k households directly; baselines are derived market-wide totals across all providers and must be multiplied by PP market share, which is unknown (parameter).
- Most plumbing and electrical multipliers and all heating multipliers are assumptions (clearly labeled) — only the cooling heat-wave effect has a published multi-shop elasticity (ServiceTitan, national, 2019–2021; Northeast not broken out).
- County household counts were not embedded: the Census ACS API now requires a key; the portal should join ACS B11001 households by county FIPS code.
- Climatology station proxies: Carlisle/Lebanon use Harrisburg Intl; Chambersburg/Gettysburg use York Airport; Toms River uses Atlantic City Intl (Lakehurst NAS daily record too sparse); Freehold COOP station has no wind-gust data.
- NWS local warning criteria for CTP (State College) and PHI (Mt Holly) were not retrievable; LWX (Sterling) criteria are used as the regional reference for heat/wind thresholds.
- Companion data /Users/syed/BSP/data/research/pp_storm_events.json holds the county-month storm history this model references.

Competitors, franchise territories, rebates and county profiles

Generated: 2026-09-24
Method: Competitors came from ZoomInfo company searches (radius around Lancaster 17601, Toms River 08753, Chambersburg 17201 and Reading 19601), Google News RSS deal searches, and fetches of each company website for founding year, reviews and ownership claims. PE and utility ownership is stated only where a deal article or company page confirms it. Franchise territories were parsed from the official One Hour, Benjamin Franklin Plumbing and Mister Sparky location directories (PA, NJ, MD, DE); each location page was fetched for rating, license and team names, and PP/Horvath affiliation is graded confirmed, likely, possible or no public evidence. Incentives come from utility, IRS and agency pages plus news of program status. County profiles use ACS 2020-2024 5-year tables (via the Census Reporter API, because api.census.gov now requires a key), Census PEP vintage 2025 county estimates, and Census Building Permits Survey 2024/2025 annual county files. Market signals are fetched news, trade-press and BLS OEWS May 2025 wage data.
Sources summary:
onehourheatandair.com / benjaminfranklinplumbing.com / mistersparky.com location directories; ZoomInfo MCP (company search); Census Reporter API (ACS 2024 5-yr); Census PEP co-est2025-alldata.csv; Census Building Permits Survey county annual files (co2024a, co2025a); BLS OEWS API (May 2025); IRS.gov; PPL Electric Savings / CLEAResult; UGI Utilities; FirstEnergy (Met-Ed, JCP&L); NJNG SAVEGREEN; NJ Clean Energy Program; PA DEP / PA Environment Digest; LancasterOnline (LNP); Central Penn Business Journal; PR Newswire; WFMZ; LebTown; WHYY; NJBIZ; NJ101.5; Homepros; ACHR News; company websites
Caveats:
- ACS data is the 2020-2024 5-year release (one vintage newer than the ACS 2023 requested), pulled from the Census Reporter mirror because api.census.gov returned 'Missing Key'. Values match Census tables but are not the 2023 vintage.
- PP ownership is confirmed only for the Lancaster (Running Pump Rd) tri-brand site and the Beachwood NJ Horvath sites. Harrisburg, York and West Chester are 'likely' (co-located tri-brand sites in counties LNP says PP serves; Franchise Times says 4 brick-and-mortar + 1 satellite). Levittown and Lansdale are 'possible'. Location pages do not name franchisees.
- A Pleasantville NJ operator also trades as 'The Punctual Pros'. No public record links it to BSP's Punctual Pros, so it is kept out of the rankings.
- The brief lists Haller Enterprises as PE-backed, but no deal announcement was found (a PitchBook snippet calls it a private company; one Glassdoor review says PE-owned). Ownership is left null and marked unverified.
- Employee counts are mostly ZoomInfo estimates and can understate multi-site firms (e.g., UGI HVAC shows 47). Review counts and ratings are shown only where a company page displayed them. Brand-wide aggregates (4.82 / 200,251 and 4.82 / 125,662) on franchise pages were set to null.
- Competitor coverage is broad in the Lancaster, Harrisburg, York, Berks and Ocean/Monmouth cores but thin in Montgomery and Chester, where many Philadelphia-suburb operators exist. Several NJ sites (Point Bay Fuel, Care Temp, A. Bailey, Premier Climate Care, Aggressive Mechanical) blocked retrieval and were excluded.
- PECO and JCP&L rebate dollar amounts could not be retrieved (page would not load for automated reading). FirstEnergy PA (Met-Ed) says it is 'working to finalize new programs' for Act 129 Phase V, so amounts are null.
- NJ HEAR/HOMES status after Sept 2025 is unverified. PA Penn Energy Savers was still 'proposed' as of July 2026.
- An apparent 'Lennar Roselyn Lancaster 1,860-unit' development in search results is in Lancaster, South Carolina, and was excluded.
- Web search quota was exhausted. Discovery used Google News RSS and ZoomInfo, and every item's primary source URL was fetched directly. Some secondary URLs (Business Wire, NJ.com, PennLive, Capital-Star, Glassdoor) returned 403 or paywalls and are cited from search results only.
- NJBIZ cites NJ DCA data showing 859 housing units authorized in Monmouth in 2025. The Census BPS county file shows 2,138 total units (1,481 single-family) for 2025. Sources and definitions differ; the county profile uses Census BPS.
- Smith + Howard (BSP's exited portfolio company) is out of scope and excluded.
- Verified 2026-09-24: sampled 24, confirmed 24, removed 0
Territory summary: 1) Punctual Pros' nine-county Central PA core (Lancaster, York, Dauphin, Cumberland, Berks, Lebanon, Franklin, Adams, Perry) holds about 2.51M people and 965k occupied homes. PP also serves the Chester, Montgomery and Bucks fringe and, through Horvath, Ocean and Monmouth counties in NJ (about 1.32M people, 496k households). 2) The housing stock is old and owner-occupied: 45-64% of units were built before 1980, median build years run 1969-1983, and owner-occupancy runs 63-82%. That is a large, recurring replacement and repair base. 3) Heating fuel splits the territory. About 241k core-PA households (and about 390k across all 13 counties) still heat with fuel oil or propane: 44.5% in Perry, 37.6% Lebanon, 30.0% Berks, 27.7% Adams, 25.2% Lancaster. Ocean and Monmouth are 78-81% utility gas. 4) Growth is concentrated in the Cumberland-York-Adams corridor (+6.9%, +3.7%, +3.6% population 2020-25) and in Ocean County (+5.7%, the most single-family permits in the footprint at 2,808 in 2024 and 2,372 in 2025). Dauphin and Monmouth are slow-growth or declining in permits. 5) PP's confirmed tri-brand sites are Lancaster (Running Pump Rd) and Beachwood NJ (Horvath). Tri-brand sites in Harrisburg, York and West Chester are likely PP. There is no One Hour / Ben Franklin / Mister Sparky location in Berks, Lebanon, Franklin, Adams or Perry. 6) Competition is densest in Lancaster, Dauphin and Chester: Haller (about 400 employees, 9.4k reviews), HB McClure (about 1,000 employees, ESOP), UGI HVAC (utility), Brubaker (ESOP). PE-backed rivals are Sila (Goldman Sachs Alternatives), Len The Plumber (Neffsville, L Catterton), P1/Essig (Berks) and Horizon (New Mountain) in the SE fringe. 7) Demand drivers for 2026 are mixed. Federal 25C/25D credits ended Dec 31, 2025, and PA's $258M Penn Energy Savers rebates remain unlaunched. Utility rebates are modest in PA (PPL heat pumps $225-325; UGI gas furnace $500, boilers $1,200-1,500; FirstEnergy PA programs in transition) but rich in NJ (NJNG SAVEGREEN up to $3,650 HVAC and $4,000 hybrid heat plus $25k 0% financing through June 30, 2027). 8) Tailwinds include record Lancaster home prices ($385k median, June 2026), rising electric rates (PPL, JCP&L), July 2026 heat-wave and flood events, and a deep technician pipeline at Thaddeus Stevens (enrollment 875 to 1,491). Local HVAC median wages are about $60-63k in PA MSAs and $78k in the NY-NJ MSA, against PP's posted $70-120k tech range.
Expansion thesis:
- Priority: 1
Move: Densify the Cumberland-York-Adams growth corridor from the Harrisburg and York sites
Evidence: Cumberland +6.9% population 2020-25 (fastest PA county in set), median sale price $369,995 (+9.5% y/y). York has the most PA single-family permits (952 in 2024, 1,025 in 2025). Adams +3.6%. York has no PE-backed competitor tracked.
Targets: Tuck-ins among West Shore and York independents: Pronto/SECCO (about 52 employees), Central Penn Plumbing (about 51 employees, 1,363 reviews), Zimmerman, Advance HAWS, RiverView Mechanical, R.D. Heller.
- Priority: 2
Move: Enter Berks (Reading) and Lebanon, whitespace for the tri-brand
Evidence: No One Hour / Ben Franklin / Mister Sparky location in Berks or Lebanon. Berks has 163k households, 63.6% built before 1980 (oldest in set), and 48.9k oil and propane homes (30.0%). Lebanon has 37.6% oil and propane and only 0.3% of homes for sale, so owners repair in place. The 537-unit Cumru Twp development and Highland Place 55+ add new-build demand. Competition is UGI HVAC plus a fragmented field; P1 already took Essig, so move before Sila (Palmyra) extends east.
Targets: Company tuck-in in Reading (e.g., Trinity Comfort about 72 employees, Gehringer Mechanical tri-trade, M&M Mechanical), paired with securing Authority Brands territory rights for Berks and Lebanon zip codes.
- Priority: 3
Move: Launch an oil and propane to heat-pump / hybrid conversion engine
Evidence: About 241k oil and propane households in the core (Lancaster 53.6k, Berks 48.9k, York 36.5k, Dauphin 24.7k, Cumberland 22.2k, Lebanon 21.3k). With 25C gone, the offer needs financing plus PPL rebates ($225-325), and UGI's $500-1,500 gas incentives where gas mains exist. Enrolling techs in DEP's Penn Heat Pump Pathways pre-qualifies PP for Penn Energy Savers (up to $8,000 per heat pump, up to $14,000 per LMI household) if DOE releases the $258M.
Targets: Service departments or customer books of fuel dealers: SOC Energy (Harrisburg/Lancaster, 1922), W.C. Eshenaur (1928), Countryside Fuel (Lebanon), Aero Energy (Adams; ESOP, so partnership is likelier than a sale).
- Priority: 4
Move: Scale Horvath from Ocean into Monmouth
Evidence: Ocean is the fastest-growing county in the footprint (+5.7%, about 36k residents 2020-25, JCP&L $108M grid build and 50+ MW of new connection requests, 2,372 single-family permits in 2025). Monmouth has the highest income ($124,845), 81% gas heat, and NJNG SAVEGREEN pays up to $3,650 HVAC and $4,000 hybrid heat with $25k 0% OBRP. Neither county has a tracked PE-backed operator.
Targets: The separate Manalapan One Hour and Mister Sparky franchisee(s) (a repeat of the Horvath franchise-to-franchise plan). Independents: Dash Mechanical (about 92 employees, Brick), Lawes (Shrewsbury, 1926), Air Experts, Garden State AC, Eastern Shore HVAC.
- Priority: 5
Move: Authority Brands franchisee roll-up in adjacent mid-Atlantic markets
Evidence: Tri-brand co-located operators near PP with strong review bases: Wilmington DE (One Hour 4.9 / 3,276; Ben Franklin 4.9 / 3,400; 410 Meco Dr), Dover DE, Bel Air/Harford MD, Mount Airy MD (One Hour 4.7 / 863), Bethlehem PA (Ben Franklin). A Pleasantville NJ operator trades as 'The Punctual Pros'; confirm whether it is related before treating it as a target.
Targets: Operators within about 90 minutes of Lancaster that already share PP's brand system, which means lower integration risk. Apex's $10B valuation (May 2026) and Sila's Goldman backing show company exit multiples reward mid-Atlantic density.
- Priority: watch
Move: Deprioritize organic push in Dauphin new construction and Franklin/Perry greenfield
Evidence: Dauphin single-family permits fell to 180 in 2025 from 287 in 2024, and HB McClure and Haller dominate. Franklin and Perry are low-density; enter via small tuck-ins or satellite trucks, not new branches.

Franchise disclosures, press, BLS and vendor data behind the nationwide plan

Title: How BSP takes Punctual Pros nationwide: Smith + Howard template, AI agents, pro programs, growth levers, expansion phases, financing
Generated: 2026-10-06
Method: Template events come from BSP, Smith + Howard and Frontline releases plus Accounting Today, CPA Practice Advisor and Inside Public Accounting coverage, fetched 2026-10-06. AI-agent, pro-program and growth-lever evidence comes from vendor case studies (ServiceTitan, Rilla, XOi, Workday Paradox, PermitFlow) and industry benchmarks (Invoca 2026, BrightLocal 2025, SearchLight Feb 2026, Ardent Partners 2025, GF Data, Synchrony). Government sources include BLS OOH 2025-35, BLS QCEW and PA L&I. Each claim was read on the cited page except where a caveat says otherwise. Expansion-phase data points were computed with python3 from repo sources: data/pp_zips.json (columnar, decoded with cols/enums/rows; core = service-territory flag 1; adjacent = adjacent to service territory 1; Tier = opportunity tier), data/research/ma_targets_pp.json (items and the Authority Brands territory map), data/research/pe_landscape.json (overlap with BSP contains 'Punctual Pros'), data/research/pp_filings.json (FDD Items 19/20, PGIM 10-Q, Form D/ADV). KPI targets and KPI roadmap are labelled analyst assumptions anchored to Punctual Pros filings' FY2025 estimates.
Caveats:
- Smith + Howard is the closest BSP precedent for a regional-to-national build. It is an Atlanta accounting and advisory firm (not a law firm) that BSP sold to TPG Growth in August 2026. Frontline Managed Services serves law firms but was already national at entry, so it appears only as a secondary analog (3 items).
- Smith + Howard has been sold, so it has no page of its own in the portal. It appears here only as the template timeline for Punctual Pros.
- Add-on count conflict: BSP's Aug 2026 release says 'nine strategic acquisitions', while BSP's Smith + Howard portfolio page lists 5 add-ons. Named transactions found: Market Street Partners, JMM CPAs, VIP Search + VIP Solutions (one transaction), Fahrenheit Advisors, Smith Kesler & Co., Horton Lee & Burnett, BPS and Geels Norton. Counting VIP Search and VIP Solutions separately reaches nine; that split is an analyst reconciliation.
- Smith + Howard entry revenue was not disclosed. Known figures are FY23 $53.2M, FY24 $74.2M and ~$175M expected for 2026; '~4x' is BSP's own claim. The India delivery center date and city are not public.
- AI-agent metrics are mostly vendor-published case studies or vendor claims (ServiceTitan, Rilla, XOi, PermitFlow, Paradox) and represent selected customers, not controlled studies. Treat them as directional upper-bound benchmarks.
- Punctual Pros' current membership count, review count, online-booking share and technician headcount are not public. Baselines marked 'analyst assumption' or null must be replaced with company data.
- Market-size figures vary by publisher: Mordor's US HVAC services estimate is $17.93B (2025) in its latest vintage and $21.16B in an older one. GMI's $26.5B is residential equipment, not services. No residential-only plumbing or electrical services size was verified.
- Richmond, VA is named in Phase 3, but data/pp_zips.json covers only PA, NJ, MD, NY and WV. So Richmond and DE have no ZIP-level figures. Authority territory counts cover only the 66 PA/NJ/MD/DE locations parsed in Punctual Pros add-on targets, not the national system.
- Expanding the franchise footprint needs Authority Brands' territory approval and transfer consent. Converting independents to franchise brands, or acquiring outside the franchise system, may face territorial restrictions not analysed here.
- Generac's ~6.5% home-standby penetration and the Frontdoor 10-K figures were taken from summaries of the filings (SEC ARS PDF; StockTitan 10-K summary), not read line by line.
Item counts by kind:
Template: 17
Ai agent: 11
Pro program: 11
Growth lever: 10
Expansion phase: 4
Financing: 6
Narrative: In about 3.7 years BSP took Smith + Howard from ~100 professionals in one Atlanta office to ~800, 11 locations, nine acquisitions and ~4x revenue, then sold to TPG Growth; Punctual Pros can follow that plan. Punctual Pros starts from a similar base: ~$22M estimated FY2025 revenue, 25 Authority Brands territories, 248 core Central-PA zips with ~1.0M housing units, and one out-of-state add-on (Horvath, Jersey Shore). Phase 1 (months 0-12) fills in the core and the 195 best nearby ZIP codes (144 PA, 51 MD). It closes 1-2 tuck-ins from the 61-company target screen. Phase 2 (months 9-24) repeats the Horvath deal across PA, NJ, MD, DE and southern NY. There, 54 mapped Authority territories are not yet owned by Punctual Pros, and 17 PE sponsors compete for the same founders. Phase 3 (18-36) builds a Mid-Atlantic hub along I-81/I-95 (Baltimore-DC, Richmond, Philadelphia suburbs, Pittsburgh), just as Fahrenheit Advisors gave Smith + Howard its first Mid-Atlantic office. Phase 4 makes Punctual Pros the national consolidator inside the One Hour / Ben Franklin / Mister Sparky system: 1,066 outlets and $831M of reported revenue, where Punctual Pros holds ~2.3% today. The redesigned website is only the front door; the real leverage is an AI layer: a 24/7 voice dispatcher (ServiceTitan reports 70% booking, 90% capacity-adjusted), missed-call text-back, AI estimating that recovered $1.2M of unsold estimates at a $20M peer, Rilla coaching that lifted a Mister Sparky's ticket 25%, AI dispatch, and back-office agents for AP, permits and recruiting. Just as important, the plan helps the pros themselves: a Thaddeus Stevens College pipeline (97% placement, 18 job opportunities per graduate), PA earn-while-you-learn apprenticeships, pay ladders and tool stipends against 16-21% annual technician turnover, AI copilots that make junior techs productive faster, and veteran hiring. That matters because BLS projects ~155,000 HVAC, plumbing and electrical openings a year nationally, so technician capacity, not demand, is the binding constraint. Growth levers stack on top: online booking, Google LSA and reviews, memberships (members spend 2.5x more), financing, generator and IAQ attach, new-mover marketing from the deed feed, and a weather-surge plan. Funding comes from the existing unitranche and its delayed-draw line, 20-35% seller rollover, Fund I follow-ons and, for larger company deals, a co-invest SPV like those for Thomas Scientific, Frontline and CET, at today's equity-heavy ~2.9-3.3x leverage. The exit thesis is multiple arbitrage plus organic growth: buy tuck-ins at ~6-7x, build a ~$100M+ revenue, AI-enabled national company, and sell it in the 10x+ tier, as Smith + Howard went to TPG.

title: Punctual Pros nationwide evidence: summary

text:
NOAA storm events recorded in the territory counties

Generated: 2026-09-24
Portfolio company: Punctual Pros (BSP) incl. Horvath Home Services (Ocean/Monmouth NJ)
Method: Downloaded NOAA NCEI Storm Events Database bulk "details" CSVs (v1.0) for data years 2019–2026 from the NCEI FTP mirror and parsed them with python3. Rows were filtered to STATE in (PENNSYLVANIA, NEW JERSEY) and to the 15 territory counties; NWS forecast-zone names (zone type Z, e.g. "EASTERN MONMOUTH", "WESTERN OCEAN", "EASTERN CHESTER") were mapped to their parent county by stripping directional prefixes. Items aggregate one row per (county, state, year, month, event type); damage strings (K/M/B) were converted to USD; injuries and deaths are direct+indirect. Seasonality uses full years 2019–2025 only; 2026 is partial (file c20260918, NCEI lags ~2–4 months).

Sources summary:
NOAA NCEI Storm Events Database bulk CSV (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/swdi/stormevents/csvfiles/); NOAA NCEI Storm Events event detail pages (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/storm-events-database/); US Census county FIPS codes
Caveats:
- Storm Events is an NWS-reported data of significant/damaging weather; it is not a complete record of every hot or cold day. Temperature-driven HVAC demand should be modeled from daily station data (see pp_demand_model.json), not event counts alone.
- Zone-based event types (Heat, Excessive Heat, Winter Storm, Winter Weather, Cold/Wind Chill, High Wind, Strong Wind, Coastal Flood, Tropical Storm) are logged per NWS forecast zone; counties split into two zones (Chester, Montgomery, Monmouth, Ocean, Atlantic, Burlington) can show two rows for one meteorological event — use episode count to de-duplicate.
- Property damage estimates are NWS/partner estimates, frequently 0 or missing for heat/cold/winter events; totals understate economic impact.
- 2026 data are partial (through the NCEI file generated 2026-09-18, typically covering events ~through May–June 2026).
- NJ Cumberland County and PA Bucks County were excluded (not in the specified territory) even though their names match or appear in zone examples.
- Companion file /Users/syed/BSP/data/research/pp_demand_model.json holds the weather-to-service-call demand model, NWS alert response plan, NWS zone/UGC/FIPS codes and weather hub points.
- Verified 2026-09-24: sampled 30, confirmed 30, removed 0 (independent re-download of all 8 NCEI bulk CSVs and full recomputation reproduced all 1,575 rows exactly — event/episode counts, damage, injuries/deaths, magnitudes, zone/county splits, sample event IDs; all 40 notable events matched source rows)

text:
Sector medians from SEC XBRL filings

Generated: 2026-09-24
Scope note: Built for the whole BSP portfolio and its public rivals, not only Punctual Pros: residential home services (Punctual Pros), commercial electrical/energy (CET / NuWave), legal/BPO managed services (Frontline; CBIZ also covers Smith + Howard), lab distribution (Thomas Scientific), communications agencies, and apparel/DTC (Fair Harbor).
Method: CIKs resolved via sec.gov/files/company_tickers.json and EDGAR company search (for delisted or renamed filers: TopBuild 1633931, WNS 1356570, Patterson 891024, Interpublic 51644). Pulled data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts for every ticker with a declared User-Agent. For each concept, took annual-duration facts (340-380 days) from 10-K/20-F filings and kept the latest-filed value per fiscal year. Revenue concept priority: Revenues > RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax > IFRS Revenue. Operating income: OperatingIncomeLoss (IFRS ProfitLossFromOperatingActivities); where not reported (FTDR, KD), pre-tax income + interest expense. Net income: NetIncomeLoss (attributable to parent). D&A: DepreciationDepletionAndAmortization / DepreciationAndAmortization, else Depreciation + AmortizationOfIntangibleAssets. EBITDA approx = operating income + D&A, unadjusted, so impairments and deal costs stay in. dei:EntityNumberOfEmployees is rarely tagged, so headcount came from each 10-K/20-F Human Capital section, text-parsed from 95 downloaded filings. Fiscal year = calendar year of period end, except Jan/Feb year-ends (LULU, DLTH), which take the prior year. Latest-year growth = latest FY vs prior FY. Revenue/employee = latest FY revenue / year-end headcount. Sector values are medians across the comps listed for that sector, except legal/BPO revenue per employee, which is the median of the onshore comps (CBIZ, Kyndryl) because offshore BPO headcount is not comparable; FIX counts in both residential and commercial.
Sources summary: SEC XBRL companyfacts API (31 companies); SEC submissions API (filing lists, 10-K URLs, 15-12G/DEFM14A/DEFA14A/S-4 events); 95 primary 10-K/20-F documents for headcount, Ameresco FY2025 statements and WPP amortisation; Federal Reserve G.5A annual average GBP/USD rates (release of 2026-01-05) for WPP conversion.
Caveats:
- All figures are GAAP/IFRS as reported and are not adjusted. EBITDA here is operating income + D&A, not company-defined Adjusted EBITDA. One-offs depress latest-year margins at AVTR (impairment), CROX (impairment), OMC (IPG deal costs), WPP (GBP 641M goodwill impairment) and TECH FY2025.
- Headcount is year-end and often rounded ('approximately', 'more than', 'over'). PRIM = salaried + hourly; DLTH = full-time + part-time; STGW = full-time only.
- Revenue per employee is not comparable across delivery models: offshore BPO runs about $18k-$35k, while pass-through distributors and project developers (PDCO, AMRC, FTDR, RVLV) run above $700k because of subcontractor or product costs.
- WPP reports under IFRS in GBP. USD values use Fed annual average rates, growth is computed in GBP, and IFRS 16 right-of-use depreciation inflates its EBITDA against US GAAP peers.
- Some comps no longer file: TopBuild (acquired by QXO, 15-12G 2026-07-13), WNS (15-12G 2025-10-27), Patterson (take-private, 15-12G 2025-04-28) and Interpublic (acquired by Omnicom, 15-12G 2025-12-08). Their latest year is their last annual report. CBIZ (Grant Thornton affiliate, $55/share cash) and Bio-Techne (Merck KGaA) have pending acquisitions.
- Ameresco's FY2025 10-K has no XBRL in companyfacts, so its FY2025 values were transcribed from the 10-K HTML.
- Kyndryl (March FYE) and Bio-Techne (June FYE) include FY2026 as the latest year. IES (Sept FYE) and WNS (March FYE) are shown on their own fiscal calendars.
- The mid-cap and large-cap public comps are 10-1000x the size of BSP's lower-middle-market companies. Use them for direction (margin structure, productivity, growth cycle), not for valuation parity.
- Allbirds now appears in EDGAR as 'Smartbird, Inc.' with the same CIK and ticker BIRD.
- Verified 2026-09-24: sampled 31, confirmed 31, removed 0

What this implies for bsp: Public residential/trade comps grew a median 13.6% in their latest year at a 14.4% operating margin (13.1% multi-year average), but the set is bimodal: installers IBP/BLD are flat (+1.0%/+1.5%) at 13-15% margins while FIX (+29.5%) and LMB (+24.7%) are growing on non-residential/data-center mechanical work, so residential-only demand is closer to low single digits. For Punctual Pros, a mid-teens EBITDA margin (IBP 15.1%, BLD 17.8%, FTDR 24.2% on an asset-light warranty model) is the realistic mature target, and a technician-led service model should sit near the ~$285k-$400k revenue/employee band of IBP, BLD and FIX. Growth above the ~2-4% revenue CAGR of the installers will need density-building tuck-ins and service-agreement/recurring revenue, which is the lever the portal's territory model should prioritize.

Margins are structurally thin, with a median operating margin of 6.4% and approximate EBITDA margin of 11.2%, and only specialist/self-perform leaders (FIX 14.4%, IESC 11.4%, EME 10.1%) clear 10%; revenue per employee clusters tightly at ~$330k-$410k (Ameresco's $1.2M reflects pass-through project costs). For CET / NuWave, that implies a benchmark of roughly $330k-$410k revenue per field+office head and a 6-10% operating margin, with upside tied to mission-critical and service/maintenance mix rather than bid-hard GC work.

Median revenue per employee basis: Onshore comps only: median of CBIZ ($290k, FY2025) and Kyndryl ($210k, FY2026), each latest-year revenue divided by year-end headcount from its annual report. The six-comp median is about $33k because the four offshore BPO comps (Genpact $35k, EXL $32k, WNS $21k, TaskUs $18k) employ mostly offshore delivery staff, which does not describe an onshore US legal-services company such as Frontline.
What this implies for bsp: BPO/managed-services comps posted a median 10.1% latest-year growth at a 12.6% operating margin and ~16.9% EBITDA margin, with TaskUs (+19.0%) and EXL (+13.6%) outgrowing Genpact (+6.6%) and WNS/Kyndryl flat. Revenue per employee is a delivery-model signal rather than a quality signal: offshore-heavy Genpact/EXL/TaskUs/WNS run $18k-$35k per head, while onshore professional-services models (CBIZ $290k, Kyndryl $210k) run 6-15x higher, so the revenue-per-employee benchmark for this sector uses the onshore comps only (about $250k). For Frontline, an onshore US legal-services model should be benchmarked on the CBIZ-type revenue/employee and 8-12% operating margins, with offshore leverage the main path toward Genpact/EXL-style 15% margins; CBIZ's pending $55/share cash sale to a Grant Thornton affiliate is also a live valuation marker for Smith + Howard-type accounting companies.

Revenue per employee for distributors runs roughly $485k-$865k (AVTR $485k, HSIC $527k, PDCO $864k), well above service businesses because product pass-through dominates revenue. For Thomas Scientific, a 4-7% EBITDA-to-revenue profile with $500k+ revenue per employee is the distribution benchmark, and margin expansion must come from proprietary/private-label mix and account penetration, since end-market volume growth is running near flat.

Reported margins are distorted by impairments and deal costs (median latest operating margin 4.2% vs a 7.8% multi-year average), while normalized holding-company margins sit around 11-15% (OMC and IPG before 2025) and revenue per employee is ~$145k-$265k. For a BSP agency portfolio company, benchmarks are roughly $190k-$265k revenue per employee and a 10-15% EBITDA margin, and growth has to come from specialist/earned-media and data capabilities because the category itself is ex-growth and consolidating.

What this implies for bsp: Apparel/DTC comps are bifurcated: the median latest-year growth is -1.5% and median operating margin 3.7%, but LULU (19.9%) and CROX (about 25-26% in FY2023-24, before its 2025 impairments) show what brand heat earns, while DLTH, RVLV and BIRD run -2% to 6% or deep losses. Allbirds (revenue down 19.7%, -52% operating margin, headcount 927 to 362 in two years) is the cautionary case for a single-category, DTC-first, sustainability-positioned footwear/apparel brand scaling stores too early. For Fair Harbor, the benchmark is roughly $275k-$500k revenue per employee and a positive high-single-digit EBITDA margin before scaling retail, with wholesale/marketplace mix (as Crocs and Revolve show) preferable to heavy owned-store build-outs.
Financial picture: 31 public peers split the BSP portfolio into three economic regimes. (1) Construction and trades (CET, Punctual Pros) lead growth: electrical/MEP comps compounded revenue at 16.8% a year (FY2023-25), versus 8.4% for residential. The trades still have thin margins, with a median operating margin of 6.4% for commercial electrical, 11.2% approximate EBITDA, and only specialists like FIX (14.4%), IESC (11.4%) and EME (10.1%) at or above 10%, so contractor value creation comes from mix (service, mission-critical) more than price. Residential comps show the split Punctual Pros faces: pure residential installers IBP and TopBuild grew only 1-1.5% in FY2025 at 13-15% operating margins, while the fast growers (FIX, LMB) are leaning on non-residential work. Frontdoor's 24% approximate EBITDA margin on about $1.03M revenue per employee shows the value of a subscription and asset-light contractor-network model in home services. (2) Services and people businesses (Frontline, Smith + Howard, the agency holding) are priced on productivity per head. Offshore BPO earns 12-15% operating margins at only $18k-$35k revenue per employee, while onshore professional services (CBIZ $290k, Kyndryl $210k) earn 3-9%. So a US-heavy legal or accounting company should expect CBIZ-like economics unless it adds offshore leverage. Agencies are ex-growth (median +0.3%, WPP -8.1% in GBP) and consolidating (Omnicom absorbed Interpublic, taking headcount from 74,900 to about 120,000), so a BSP agency asset has to win on specialist growth rather than category tailwind. (3) Product businesses (Thomas Scientific, Fair Harbor) are scale-and-mix stories. Lab distribution grows at a median 1.5% with 4-5% operating margins for pure distributors (HSIC, PDCO), against 17-21% for manufacturers (TMO, TECH), so private-label and proprietary content are the margin lever for Thomas Scientific. Apparel/DTC is the most dispersed sector: LULU earns about 20% operating margin, but Duluth and Allbirds show negative margins and shrinking revenue, and Allbirds went from 927 to 362 employees in two years. For Fair Harbor, capital discipline around retail expansion matters more than top-line speed. Finally, M&A activity among the comps (QXO/TopBuild, the WNS and Patterson take-outs in 2025, Omnicom/Interpublic, Grant Thornton affiliate/CBIZ at $55 cash, Merck KGaA/Bio-Techne) signals active strategic and sponsor demand in four of BSP's six sectors, which supports exit optionality for the portfolio.

- BDC/N-PORT holdings show only one lender's slice of each facility; total facility size, and therefore leverage and EBITDA, cannot be observed directly. Implied EBITDA ranges are analyst estimates.
- PPP figures are from 2020–21 and predate most PE roll-ups; they describe the predecessor operating company, not the current company.

Financial picture:
- Home services is splitting in two. The scaled companies (Wrench, Apex, Redwood, Legacy) borrow at S+425–475, marked at par, with delayed-draw lines for acquisitions. The next tier (TurnPoint, Horizon, Any Hour, Len the Plumber) has moved to part PIK interest and is marked at 89–94. Lenders are paying for scale and punishing leverage taken on at 2021-era prices.
- Punctual Pros' PA/NJ/DE footprint is exposed to the stressed side: Horizon Services (HGH Purchaser) has at least $211M of first lien at Blue Owl alone, paying 3.75% PIK, marked 92.5, with lenders also holding its common equity. Heartland's debt matures Dec 15, 2026. So two regional competitors are likely to sell assets or be restructured in the next 12 months rather than bid aggressively for add-ons.
- Sila (King of Prussia) and Haller (Lancaster, 254 trucks) are the healthier local rivals. Sila's 2,500+ employees imply about $0.45–0.65B revenue, versus a single ~96-person company in its 2020 PPP record, so its growth has come almost entirely from acquisitions.
- For CET, IES's Commercial & Industrial segment is the cleanest margin benchmark: $427.7M revenue, 20.3% gross margin, 11.0% operating margin, and backlog that doubled to $625.2M. Across the whole company, IES earns 11.4% operating margins with no net debt, so it can pay strategic prices for New England contractors.
- PPP data puts CET's largest private MA competitors at about $100–135M (Interstate Electrical: $8.57M loan, 500 jobs, ~$41.1M payroll costs) and at least $120–160M (J&M Brown: $10M capped loan, 445 jobs, payroll costs of at least $48M). Both are family-owned union contractors with no lender filings, so they compete on labor capacity rather than on capital.
- Legal services lenders are signaling real stress. Consilio's term loan fell from 90.95 to 77.85–82.94 in the first half of 2026 with a May 2028 maturity, and Epiq's (DTI Holdco) traded at 89–93. That is consistent with AI compressing managed-review and eDiscovery revenue, and it weakens two large vendors that compete with Frontline for law-firm technology budgets.
- Integreon (WhiteHorse/Twin Brook unitranche, S+550, June 2027 maturity) and Kraft Kennedy (about 100 staff and ~$7.5M payroll in 2020, implying ~$20–30M revenue) are the rivals closest to Frontline in size. Kraft Kennedy's SOC/security push matches the upsell path Frontline is pursuing with AmLaw firms.
- In lab distribution, Avantor's $785M goodwill impairment on VWR, 4.6% Lab Solutions sales decline and 10.2% Q2-2026 adjusted operating margin at VWR Distribution & Services give Thomas Scientific a vulnerable category leader to take share from and a realistic margin ceiling. Calibre Scientific (S+600 debt maturing June 2027, CEO departed March 2026) looks like a 2026–27 refinancing or sale.
- In strategic communications, KKR's $1.7B enterprise value for FGS (WPP stake $775M), financed with an S+450 unitranche, sets a premium valuation. Precision Strategies' new March-2026 leverage facility (about $10.7M visible at Stellus) shows sponsors are now financing mid-size Democratic-aligned agencies like BPI.
- Stagwell's Communications segment (SKDK) lost 16.5% of organic net revenue in 2025, and advocacy alone fell $62.7M. That quantifies the election-cycle swing BPI should expect: a sharp off-year decline followed by an 11% consolidated revenue recovery in Q2 2026 heading into the midterms.
- In apparel, Chubbies (Fair Harbor's closest public comparison) earned about $22.4M of segment contribution on $122.9M of FY2025 sales (57.9% gross margin). But Q2-2026 DTC sales fell 20.8%, and its parent Solo Brands was delisted from the NYSE in July 2026 with about $249M of debt, so a Chubbies sale is plausible. Private Vuori and Outerknown left no SEC or PPP trace.

text:
Evidence for tech-enabled multiples and the roadmap assumptions

Generated: 2026-10-06
Scope note: Six active BSP portfolio companies. Smith + Howard (exited to TPG, Aug 2026) is excluded. CET guidance: no NYC expansion; GridOS is New England only.
Method: Web research on 2026-10-06 (search plus direct fetches of press releases, SEC filings, banker reports and vendor pages), combined with existing verified portal sources (public comparables, Punctual Pros market research, Punctual Pros filings, CET filings, Frontline filings, Thomas Scientific filings, BPI filings, rival filings, Fair Harbor filings). Each valuation evidence item states its number and source; derived arithmetic (e.g., members per technician, implied EV/revenue) is labelled "derived". KPI benchmark baselines and targets come from sourced benchmarks; where a company actual is not public, baseline or target is null. roadmap assumption items are explicit analyst assumptions (labelled est.) tied by evidence links to items in this file; USD EBITDA impact = low/high revenue estimate x low/high margin points.
Item counts:
Valuation evidence: 26
Vendor stack: 28
Kpi benchmark: 20
Roadmap assumption: 6
Caveats:
- Reported deal multiples (Champions 18.5x, Sila ~17x) are press estimates from people familiar with the deals; sponsors did not disclose terms.
- Multiples for scaled roll-ups mostly reflect scale, density and M&A runway, not technology alone. This file credits only a fraction of the typical-to-premium spread to tech enablement.
- Vendor case studies (ServiceTitan Pricebook Pro, Rilla, Avoca, True Fit, Bold Metrics, Rewst) are self-reported, self-selected and unaudited; treat them as upper bounds.
- Portfolio company revenue/EBITDA figures are low-confidence analyst estimates from the portal filings sources, not company disclosures.
- Vendor pricing marked third-party comes from pricing-guide sites and may be stale; confirm with vendors before budgeting.
- MetricNet first-level-resolution and cost-per-ticket figures date from 2011 and are directional only.
- The ServiceTitan TitanAdvisor quartile figure (20% vs 8%) was taken from S-1 search extraction; the direct fetch confirmed other S-1 figures but not this one.
- Thomas Scientific's capital structure (est. 7-10x leverage, Dec-2027 maturity) dominates its exit value; LabOS multiple expansion is secondary to EBITDA and refinancing.
Thesis summary: BSP's six active companies are services businesses whose exit multiples depend on how predictable, recurring and scalable their earnings look to the next buyer. Banker data show this directly: PKF puts project-heavy, low-retention HVAC firms at 5-6x EBITDA and repeatable-service firms with value-enhancing in-house capabilities at 10x+, and Capstone/IMAP expect a 3.0-turn spread between typical (6.8x) and premium (9.8x) middle-market deals. Each "OS" is a named, buyer-legible operating system assembled mostly from proven vendors (ServiceTitan, Procore, ConnectWise/Kaseya, Shopify Plus/Coupa, Brandwatch/Zignal, Shopify/Klaviyo) plus a thin BSP data layer from the portal, not custom software. ServiceOS for Punctual Pros is the lead case: HVAC call booking rates average 38% versus 59% at 25+ technician shops, pricebook adopters grew tickets 14% vs 8%, and scaled membership-dense companies (Champions ~18.5x, Sila ~17x) are where the premium sits. GridOS (CET) and FirmOS (Frontline) turn project and ticket work into measured, recurring service lines (solar/SCADA O&M, security and e-billing revenue cycle), the attributes PKF and Aventis say buyers pay for. LabOS (Thomas Scientific) is an EBITDA and cost-to-serve program benchmarked to Avantor's ~80% digital transactions and Grainger's ~15.6% digital growth vs ~2% rep-led growth, because leverage, not multiple, drives that exit. SignalOS (BPI) and HarborOS (Fair Harbor) productize monitoring and retention, following Stagwell's Marketing Cloud (+230%) and DTC retention economics (5 points of retention lifting profit 25-95%, per Bain). Across the six, analyst assumptions total roughly $6.0-12.4M of investment for 0.5-5 points of EBITDA margin and 0.5-2.5 turns of EBITDA multiple (0.2-0.5x revenue for Fair Harbor), each tied to sourced evidence and labelled est.
Multiple premium summary:
Headline: Up to ~3 turns of EBITDA is the quality premium the evidence supports for recurring, visible, tech-enabled services earnings. Tech enablement can claim about 0.5-2.5 turns of it, depending on the company; 17-20x roll-up prints come from scale.
By platform:
Pp:

1; 2.5
Support: PKF 5-6x vs 10x+ grid; Capstone 6.8x vs 9.8x; Champions ~18.5x and Sila ~17x at scale; ServiceTitan heavy users grow GTV 20% vs 8%.
Strength: strong for direction, medium for size
Cet:
Range turns:
0.5; 1.5
Support: PKF grid (service mix, retention, in-house capabilities); Capstone spread; electrical M&A slowed to 99 deals in 2025 (buyers more selective); Procore 95% GRR.
Strength: medium

0.5; 1.5
Support: Aventis MSP size curve 5.2x to 11.2x and churn/recurring drivers; entry already ~12-15x (est.); Kaseya security-driven margins; Clio legal-software valuation.
Strength: medium
Ts:

0.5; 1
Support: Avantor ~80% digital transactions and Grainger digital growth support EBITDA/growth, not a disclosed multiple premium; capital structure dominates.
Strength: weak for multiple, medium for EBITDA
Bpi:

0.5; 2
Support: PPHC ~8.4x floor vs 10-13x estimated sponsor exit; FGS $1.7B EV; Stagwell Marketing Cloud +230%; Publicis +5.6% organic vs WPP decline.

What it does not support: No source isolates a pure "technology premium" with a control group; the premiums observed bundle scale, recurring mix, margin and growth. Use the ranges as analyst assumptions in the techos calculator, not as market facts.
Public comps tie in: See data/research/public_comps.json sector benchmarks: residential home services median EBITDA margin 15.1% (Frontdoor 24.2% on a membership model); commercial electrical median 11.2%; legal/BPO managed services 16.9%; communications agencies and apparel DTC are bimodal (Publicis/LULU vs WPP/smaller DTC).

Phases, levers, AI agents and the roadmap for Thomas Scientific

Title: Thomas Scientific: the growth plan
Generated: 2026-10-06
Subject: Thomas Scientific (Swedesboro NJ; BSP portfolio company since Jan 2022)
Thesis: From distributor to lab-supply-chain company: target-account selling into 27.5k scored lab and hospital sites, punchout ordering, VMI, private label and specialty verticals; regional add-ons; AI agents for quoting, forecasting and account health.
Method: Expansion-phase data points are computed from repo sources: data/ts_sites.json (27,503 sites, aggregated by region only: counts by vertical, priority label and archetype, and summed 2023 CMS allowed amounts), data/ts_parents.json (top 500 parents), data/research/ma_targets_fl_ts.json (25 Thomas Scientific targets, ZoomInfo revenue estimates), Thomas Scientific filings (capital structure and estimates), public comparables (lab-distribution medians), PE landscape (Calibre, Sterling), BSP firm profile (Smith + Howard timeline and Thomas add-ons) and ServiceOS evidence (LabOS KPI benchmarks kb-ts-1..3, ve-06, ra-ts). External evidence was gathered on 2026-10-06 by web search and direct fetches of SEC filings (Avantor FY2025 10-K, VWR FY2014 10-K), state/federal pages (NJDOL), banker reports (Houlihan Lokey) and vendor case studies. Growth-lever and KPI targets are benchmarks or labelled assumptions; the KPI roadmap is an analyst assumption anchored to the Thomas Scientific filings estimate table.
Caveats:
- Thomas Scientific's first-lien loan matures December 14, 2027 (88.3% of par in the lender's June 2026 10-Q); est. leverage 7-10x. Every lever is sequenced behind liquidity and refinancing.
- Company revenue, EBITDA and headcount are low-confidence analyst estimates (Thomas Scientific filings), not company disclosures; the KPI roadmap inherits that uncertainty.
- data/research/market_evidence.json and a KPI targets data were not present in the repo at build time; KPI targets use ServiceOS evidence KPI benchmark items (kb-ts-*) and external sources, labelled as assumptions.
- Thomas lab-site list scores are from a legacy targeting tool (NPPES, CMS 2023, CLIA, Hospital Compare); site counts are aggregated by region only, and the CMS allowed amount is Medicare billing, not lab-supply spend.
- Vendor case studies (InstaLILY, Conexiom, Algolia, Conga/PROS, HighRadius, Flagship VMI) are self-reported and unaudited; treat them as upper bounds. weeks to deploy values are analyst estimates.
- Market-size figures for cleanroom, cannabis testing and healthcare cold chain come from market-research firms whose forecasts vary widely.
- The McKinsey forecasting figures and the Antylia/GTCR details come from search-engine extracts because the primary pages blocked automated fetches.
- ZoomInfo revenue estimates for add-on targets are modeled and can be far off.
Item counts:
Template: 9
Expansion phase: 4
Growth lever: 10
Ai agent: 9
Talent program: 6
Financing: 5
Narrative:
- Thomas is BSP's first deal; its first-lien loan matures in December 2027 (88% of par in the lender's June 2026 10-Q).
- This plan puts cash and refinancing first and growth second; the growth story is what earns the refinancing.
- Smith + Howard shows the shape: a regional leader that grew from about 100 to 800 people, 1 to 11 locations and nearly 4x revenue through nine add-ons, specialist capabilities and technology investment.
- For Thomas the equivalent is not 4x revenue; it is turning a 125-year-old distributor into a lab supply-chain portfolio company that buyers value above a commodity distributor.
- The demand map already exists: 27,503 scored lab, pathology and hospital sites, 713 rated Pursue and 2,317 Nurture, and the top 500 parent organizations account for 832 of the scored sites.
- An inside-sales academy on Grainger's model, with 4 weeks of training and then a 100-account book, would need about 30 books to cover every Pursue and Nurture site.
- Digital is table stakes: Avantor does about 80% of transactions online, and Grainger's ePro channels are about 40% of connected orders, growing far faster than rep-led sales.
- Margin has to come from mix: private label was 19% of VWR's sales at higher margins, AI pricing tools have added about 120 basis points at large distributors, and VMI makes accounts sticky.
- Cleanroom, cannabis-testing, cold-chain and forensics programs add faster-growing niches on top of a lab-distribution market growing about 1.5% a year.
- AI agents for quoting, order entry, search, forecasting, collections and account health are cheap relative to the cash they release; each day of DSO is worth about $0.8M.
- Add-ons restart only when funded: one $15-25M regional or specialty distributor a year (Midland, MIDSCI, Capitol, Valutek, Genesee), competing mainly against Calibre Scientific.
- On our assumptions EBITDA moves from about $30M to about $42.5M in 36 months, which brings leverage back near 6x and inside today's unitranche market, the bar for an amend-and-extend, recap or sale.

What broad sky can copy: Horizon is the closest-geography cautionary tale: a fast-growing DE/PA/NJ brand that doubled headcount in two years under Sun, was sold on to New Mountain, and by 2026 was paying interest in kind and partly owned by its lenders. Title: How sponsors created value in home-services and adjacent companies: merged case set, common levers, chronological patterns and a dated Punctual Pros sequence
Generated: 2026-10-06
Author: Syed Rahman
Source files:
data/research/cases_home_services.json; data/research/cases_cross_sector.json; data/research/pp_nationwide.json; data/research/serviceos_evidence.json; data/research/pe_landscape.json; data/research/pp_filings.json
Method: Merged the 17 home-services cases (cases_home_services.json) and 17 cross-sector cases (cases_cross_sector.json) into one set. De-duplication was by normalised company name; no company appeared in both files, so all 34 cases are kept with every original field preserved. Each case gains confidence (high = SEC/Companies House filings or sponsor releases with disclosed figures; medium = sponsor/company releases and trade press with figures undisclosed or press-estimated; low = few primary sources or reliance on search summaries), confidence basis, related cases, PE landscape links (sponsor ids in pe_landscape.json) and, where one exists, a portal view. Levers and patterns were derived from the dated timelines, levers used and KPI before/after of the 34 cases; every evidence row carries the source URL of the case timeline or KPI it came from. Timing statistics were computed in Python from timeline dates (months = days / 30.44; year-only dates use 1 July). Cross-references to Punctual Pros nationwide plan (pn-*), ServiceOS evidence (ve-*, kb-*) and Punctual Pros filings (pp-fil-*) reuse those items' source URL and retrieved dates. No new web retrieval was done for this merge; underlying pages were retrieved 2026-10-06 (BDC loan marks and Punctual Pros filings items 2026-09-24).
Caveats:
- Almost no sponsor discloses entry or exit EV, EBITDA or MOIC. The only exit multiples in the multiple fields are press estimates: Champions ~18.5x (Bloomberg-cited) and Sila ~17x incl. pending acquisitions (HomePros). Apex ~20x and FGS ~19x are analyst arithmetic and stay out of the multiple fields.
- revenue growth multiple uses only sourced before/after pairs or sponsor-stated multiples (TurnPoint ~10x, Smith + Howard ~4x, Sciens >35x, Shermco 2x, Teneo >2x); several are not like-for-like (perimeter changes, systemwide sales instead of revenue), as stated in each row note.
- Timing statistics are small samples: first add-on n=11, cadence n=8, hold n=21. First-add-on months exclude cases whose earliest add-ons are missing from the sources (e.g. Apex, Sila under MSCP, Heartland).
- Hold years measure the case's entry date to exit date, i.e. the first sponsor in the case fields (e.g. Odyssey for Champions, MSCP for Sila, GI Partners for Consilio).
- VWR (cx-09) and Avantor (cx-10) share the 2017 transaction; both are kept and cross-linked. Wrench (case-wr) and Apex (case-ap) share Alpine's growth plan. Smith + Howard (cx-01) also appears as template items pn-tpl-* in pp_nationwide.json.
- No case gives a sourced "share of customers on a membership" figure, so the membership pattern uses members per technician (Champions) and memberships per household served (Redwood/Sierra, derived).
- Vendor case studies (ServiceTitan, Rilla) and benchmarks cross-referenced from ServiceOS evidence and Punctual Pros nationwide plan are selected customers or vendor data, not controlled studies.
- Punctual Pros applicability, Punctual Pros next step and the Punctual Pros sequence are analyst recommendations, not company plans. Steps 0-2 are dated facts; steps 3-14 are proposed. Punctual Pros KPIs (members, booking rate, close rate) are not public and must come from its ServiceTitan.
